title: An SNL Exchange That Captures the AI Disconnect
excerpt: Saturday Night Live kicked off Season 52 last night with its version of a big interview: Partway through “Weekend Update , ” the co-anchor Michael Che brought o
body: Saturday Night Live kicked off Season 52 last night with its version of a big interview: Partway through “Weekend Update , ” the co-anchor Michael Che brought on the Anthropic CEO and co-founder Dario Amodei (played by the cast member Jane Wickline) to address the crowd
Amodei would presumably use the moment to put viewers at ease about AI, after multiple high-profile incidents raised fears about the technology escaping human control

Earlier this month, the real Amodei had published a nearly 4,000-word paper arguing that the industry needed to pace itself; here, SNL imagined, was another big opportunity to appeal to an audience, assuaging their fears of AI’s growth while standing up for his company’s product, Claude. “Weekend Update” hardly quelled any lingering concerns

Wickline, as Amodei, was bedecked in the co-founder’s signature round spectacles and white V-neck tee tucked under a cardigan—the same outfit that he wore during a sit-down interview with CBS Sunday Morning after the paper’s release

Amodei offered a weak attempt at reassurance: “I may have been alarming in my recent interviews, but I want to assure you that if we can pressure lawmakers to create guardrails, we will be able to stop me.” When Che followed up with a question that Amodei should have been prepared for—“Can you just explain how your company isn’t going to kill us?”—the tech entrepreneur rocked back and forth for a few moments

Finally, after haltingly repeating the word so to buy time, he offered a nonresponse: “That’s a really hard question.” Amodei may not be an obvious impression for Wickline, now in her third year on the show
During her previous two seasons, Saturday Night Live seemed unsure of how to best make use of her comedic gifts
A former TikToker known for monotone musical comedy and awkwardly staged micro-sketches, Wickline was hired in 2024
The decision was divisive among fans; some chafed at her dry line readings and deadpan expressions, while others adored the flecks of zany unpredictability

But Wickline’s take on Amodei deftly showcased her talents, as she nailed little details that have come to distinguish Amodei: his small smile that gives way to a smirk; nervy mannerisms, such as visibly tensed shoulders

In a touch especially keyed to her wackier sensibilities, Wickline played Amodei as someone torn between two selves—akin to the Lord of the Rings character Sméagol, whose obsession with the titular ring causes him to lose himself in the process and leads to the emergence of an id-driven personality known as Gollum . “Come on Dario,” Wickline’s Amodei said to himself at one point, his voice lilting with doubt. “Just reassure them.” His Gollum-esque other-self then responded with a growl, “I will.” Wickline’s Amodei continued to flail throughout the interview, even as Che began to ask seemingly simple questions about AI’s benefits

The Anthropic co-founder failed to name a single one—a telling portrait of industry giants’ struggle to excite the progressively more worried public about AI’s potential as experts continue to caution users of the possible damage these products could inflict upon society

Those experts include AI companies’ own employees, past and present: One former Anthropic researcher warned grimly that the technology might “kill us all by the end of the decade,” adding that AI founders were apparently well acquainted with these risks; a current Anthropic safety researcher chimed in to claim that there was a more than 10 percent chance that AI could “kill all humans.” Wickline’s Amodei, asked to explain how AI is supposed to make life better, offered Che a metaphor. “It’s simple,” he said. “If you could drink a milk that made your life easier, but there was a 10 percent chance it killed you, would you drink the milk?” He seemed shocked when Che immediately said no.

title: What Is the Meaning of Mystical Experience?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube What would it be like to wake up one day with the ability to greet the world with warmth, patience, grace, an
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube What would it be like to wake up one day with the ability to greet the world with warmth, patience, grace, and affection? This is what happens to the main character in the Pulitzer Prize winner Ayad Akhtar’s magnificent new novel, The Radiance
It is a tale of spiritual transformation in which Akhtar gives a detailed description of our inner landscapes
David and Akhtar talk about what it’s like to see the world with new eyes, and how difficult it is to move from the head to the heart
The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Ayad Akhtar is one of America’s leading playwrights and writers
His plays, like The Disgraced , which won the Pulitzer Prize, and his earlier novels, including Homeland Elegies , often describe what it’s like to be a Muslim American in the post-9/11 era
His characters, Muslim and non-Muslim alike, are often coping with rage, pressure, resentments, hostility, a feeling of being judged
His new novel, The Radiance , is about a man whose spiritual state is transformed, who begins to radiate a glow which emerges from a kind of inner illumination
You could say he becomes one of those incandescent people you meet from time to time
I’m not exaggerating when I say it’s something of a masterpiece
The book brilliantly puts into words that most ineffable thing—spiritual sensations and experience
If you read it, which of course I recommend, you’ll be led on a tour through those deep inner places that most of us struggle to see and understand
When I started doing this podcast, I thought I’d have great conversations at an intellectual and emotional level that I feel comfortable with
But now, as I prepare to talk with Ayad, I feel like a person who’s about to jump off a high dive into a bottomless pool even though he can’t swim
I’m nervous and even a little afraid because I’m gonna talk to someone who knows about the realms I struggle to see and understand
I’m beginning to get the sense that this job is going to demand that I enlarge and deepen myself in ways that I hadn’t planned for but may end up doing me some good in the end
If you come along for the ride, I think the conversation will have the same effect on you
I’m David Brooks, and this is The Permanent Questions
Brooks: Ayad Akhtar, welcome to The Permanent Questions

Brooks: On the cover of your book is a blurb by Abraham Verghese, who wrote The Covenant of Water and other things, and the blurb is: “Simply put, a work of genius.” And when I read that— Akhtar: I’m sorry. ( Laughs .) Brooks: —of course I wanted to kill you
But, I thought, Well, I’m a little suspicious
But this book, simply put, is a work of genius
I think it’s just gonna be one of the important books
You know, it’s been a few years since we’ve had a novel that was really a literary occasion

And I’d say this book is that literary occasion, in part because of the stuff we’ll talk about, but in part because we’ve lived in an era where so many spiritual poisons have been let loose by politics, by technology, by the general rancor
And here’s a book that takes spiritual life seriously and really lays out the inner world and describes a landscape of it
And I have to say, I’m a little intimidated, because I try to think about the spiritual life, but it’s all a little fuzzy down there

I think one of the things the book did for me was give me words to describe some of the things you vaguely feel, and also just to think, Well, how does spiritual life develop and grow? And so I guess, my first simple question is: Describe the premise and the concept of the novel

Akhtar: So a writer who has my name and many of the facts of my life—which is something I’m sure we’ll talk a little bit about—leaves the city after writing a previous book in which he had done the same thing, given the narrator his name and many of the facts of his life, and moves to the country

And after being there for a while, is out on a country road on a bike and gets hit by a pickup truck from behind, thrown into a grove of trees, and wakes up in a hospital after a coma about 36 hours later
And as he awakens into himself, something’s changed
There’s a luminosity and a silence that is the ground of his experience
And then that experience seems to deepen and get more complex over the subsequent eight months
And the book basically tracks that eight-month period
Simultaneously to this, he also has a friend who is teaching at a local college where he is asked to teach as well for a semester

And so the ongoing political divisions on campus, as well as within the local rural community, play a significant role as our narrator experiences what some friend of mine once called, in reading it, something like a “beatitude” or a “state of grace.” Brooks: He’s luminous, he’s incandescent, and he’s having a great time
And the first thing I love about his state of consciousness is that it’s about perception
And the very beginning of the book, before you even get to the chapters, the sentence is: “This is a record of altered perceptions.” Akhtar: Yeah
Brooks: And what I like about that is, we used to think perception, the act of seeing the world, was this passive thing
You open your eyes, the world floods in, and you record it the way an old camera would record light
We now know from neuroscience that’s not the way it happens

title: The Kennedy Center Is the Most Terrifying Building in America
excerpt: Don’t you dare go inside the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts! It’s much too dangerous
body: Don’t you dare go inside the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts! It’s much too dangerous
They have had murders there for 39 straight years —every night, and some matinees too
And they still haven’t caught the culprit
Nightly murders, with groups of middle schoolers sitting there, applauding
Murders in a hair salon, of all places! Sheer madness
It is not just the murder capital of Washington
They built a barricade on one of the stages and tried to take down the whole French government
This is the kind of thing that the Kennedy Center harbors and abets
They shot Alexander Hamilton there, not just once, but nightly, to make sure he was really dead
People went Into the Woods and got trampled by a giant
Fairies forced people to fall in love, then out of love
The falling ceiling is the least of anyone’s concerns
Everything else about this place is far more threatening
And it’s not just murders and revolutions and dancing rodents
They tested out new technologies there, called “plays.” (They even tested a couple of mine .) People got handed sheets of paper to read from and stood behind music stands and became other people
A very dangerous device, the play, and the Kennedy Center encouraged it
The most diabolical thing was that you did not always need to pay for these things
They just gave them away, free, every afternoon, for decades, to anyone who wanted to come in and watch
They gave them away online too! And nobody prevented this! This place encouraged other, equally frightening things
These performers didn’t even speak with words, just moved their bodies around and blew wind through metal tubes and reeds and scratched at strings—and people left the room in tears
What was the music saying? What were the bodies saying? The audience seemed to understand, but there were no words to help them
If people can communicate like this, then how can speech be properly controlled? If people can understand one another just by scratching a bow across taut strings—perhaps this is a form of witchcraft
No place that tolerates it must be permitted to stand
Dancing? Kicking? There was ambiguity, and that was scary
Sometimes they watched movies on the lawn outside
They gathered together and experienced things together, and that, we can agree, was dangerous
There was comedy and drama and voices you only dreamed of hearing in person
People learned things of which they had been previously unaware
There were chimes and fountains and overpriced intermission snacks
They dared to invite children into this place too
They dared to sit them down and tell them stories, on a stage
Do you know what a story can do to a mind? Do you know how long that story can linger before exploding into life, decades later? The Kennedy Center is the deadliest condemned building in America
For 55 years, people have been going in and coming out changed
Not physically, not visibly, but inside, carrying dangerous stories with them
Carrying music that could sustain them through times of trial, or the encouragement of shared laughter, or the seditious sense that they were not alone
Root it out! Stamp it out! Knock it down with a wrecking ball! This building is much too dangerous.

title: The Hidden State Russia Is Building Inside Ukraine
excerpt: T he world has watched Russia’s war against Ukraine largely through the movement of its front lines
body: T he world has watched Russia’s war against Ukraine largely through the movement of its front lines
But behind those lines, Moscow is building something more durable: a hidden state inside Ukraine
Across the Russian-occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson, Russian institutions are steadily replacing Ukrainian ones and reshaping the routines of everyday life
Official documents, such as mandated Russian passports, tie residents to the Russian state
Russian systems govern access to housing and public services
On June 13, Vladimir Putin told Russian officials that Moscow’s task is to unify these Ukrainian territories into a legal, economic, educational, cultural, and information space under Russia by 2030
The objective is permanence: to make Ukrainian civic life hard to maintain and Russian rule hard to undo
This agenda predates the full-scale invasion of Ukraine
Crimea became an early laboratory for it after Russia annexed the peninsula, in 2014
Moscow quickly imposed Russian citizenship on Crimeans and made documentation—most commonly passports—necessary for employment and access to basic services

It introduced Russian law in Crimea and replaced Ukrainian institutions with Russian ones. [ Read: Russia’s real strategy in Europe ] The Ukrainian territories occupied after the 2022 invasion have been more difficult to wrangle
The eastern provinces house major industrial assets, hundreds of thousands of people who consider themselves Ukrainians, and active resistance networks
Moscow initially relied heavily on occupation administrations, military coercion, and improvised measures
Gradually, however, it has introduced a more durable architecture to yoke the territories to the Russian state
R ussia has extended the dominion of its administrative state across occupied Ukraine
Russian federal courts claim jurisdiction there, and Russian taxation, migration, security, and military apparatuses hold authority

In 2025, Moscow integrated the occupation administrations into the monitoring software it calls the Governor’s Dashboard, which keeps track of local construction projects, budgets, and administrative compliance in real time across Russia
One aim of this integration is to sever occupied Ukraine from Kyiv and pull its residents firmly under Russian oversight and control
Ukrainians are required to get Russian passports, without which they cannot receive pensions, get jobs, collect state benefits, or pursue studies
They can’t even use phones: Local mobile operators now require Russian identity documents for SIM cards

A young man who left Kherson because he feared being detained for his pro-Ukrainian views, or conscripted into the Russian military, described how he was forced to obtain a Russian passport. “They put a gun to my head,” he told us
Like other Ukrainians we spoke to from these territories, he asked that his name be withheld for fear of retaliation against his loved ones
Many Ukrainians living under occupation have become convinced that independent Ukraine is unreachable
Russia took, replaced, or made unusable the Ukrainian documents that residents once had
Sophia, a 24-year-old from occupied Donetsk, told us that the occupation authorities repeatedly informed residents that Kyiv had abandoned them, and that only Moscow would issue them passports now
Without documents, Sophia felt trapped: Russia “was the only place I could legally go,” she said, even though she did not want to live there
To men aged 18 to 65, Russian citizenship brings military registration and punishment for noncompliance
From February 2022 to the end of 2025, in direct violation of international humanitarian law, the Russian army forcibly mobilized approximately 50,000 Ukrainians to fight against their own country
At the same time, Russia has been systematically expropriating Ukrainians’ property
Many who fled the territories under Russian occupation left real estate behind
Some of their homes have been classified as ownerless or unregistered, paving the way for their confiscation
Those who wish to retain their property must reregister it under Russian law by the end of the year
Doing so requires Russian citizenship and personally returning to the occupied territory
Since 2024, Russian authorities have confiscated , or identified for confiscation, at least 34,000 properties belonging to Ukrainian citizens

And they have begun allocating some of these homes to Russian citizens, whom they encourage to settle in occupied Ukraine, with the alleged goal of increasing the territories’ total number of Russians to 1 million by 2045
This year, occupation authorities began transferring plots of Ukrainian land to Russians, with preference given to servicemen and those who have signed military contracts
T he state that Moscow is building in occupied Ukraine is more isolated and poorer than the one from which it was wrenched

Since 2022, Moscow has worked to cut off the occupied regions from the Ukrainian information space by blocking independent media, restricting messaging services, and replacing the communications infrastructure with Russian-controlled networks
Hundreds of Ukrainian and independent websites are inaccessible, and residents struggle to access Telegram, WhatsApp, and VPNs
Since 2022, Moscow has poured billions of dollars into reconstructing occupied Ukraine

title: Why Empathy Is Now ‘Toxic,’ ‘Suicidal,’ and a ‘Sin’
excerpt: ET on September 27, 2026 A crusade against empathy is sweeping through the right
body: ET on September 27, 2026 A crusade against empathy is sweeping through the right
In sometimes apocalyptic terms, prominent conservatives are denouncing that feeble human capacity to understand the feelings of others

This is a trend I’ve written about before, but I’ve been intrigued by the way these figures have lately been adopting the language of the Canadian marketing professor Gad Saad and his influential book, Suicidal Empathy , released earlier this year

According to Saad, suicidal empathy is when otherwise positive impulses are “hijacked and used to make policy decisions that are best tackled via a sober analysis”—a phenomenon that will lead to nothing less than “the collective suicide of the West.” Like other works in this growing genre, including Paul Bloom’s Against Empathy , Allie Beth Stuckey’s Toxic Empathy , and Joe Rigney’s The Sin of Empathy , Saad’s book contends that a progressive fixation on oppressed groups in the name of compassion and fairness has been not just counterproductive but also destructive, threatening Western values and even civilization itself
Robert Barron, a Roman Catholic bishop and podcaster in Minnesota, recently took up Saad’s argument in an episode that contrasted suicidal empathy with Christian charity
Barron calmly explained that love, far from mandating kindness, can and often should be harsh
This is a classic right-wing talking point: Conservatives have long argued that refusing to offer social-welfare programs, for example, is a way of teaching the dignity of self-reliance

To sideline traditionally conservative values in favor of allegedly empathy-driven liberal causes is, in Barron’s view, to “undermine the foundations of the West.” Although I have heard versions of this before, I was still surprised to hear a prelate of the Catholic Church arguing that people should not be empathetic if doing so could come at considerable personal or societal cost
Barron has more than 3.6 million YouTube subscribers, 675,000 Instagram followers, and—as of last week—a presidential appointment to the U.S
Commission on International Religious Freedom
His Christian commitments and considerable influence make his interest in these ideas notable
But his reasoning seems more political than spiritual
Suicidal Empathy and books like it are aimed not at liberals, but at conservatives who may be struggling with a conflict between their politics and their conscience

Arguments about the harms of empathy help justify personal and political behavior that might otherwise seem wrong or feel bad, such as cutting food-stamp benefits for poor people or tearing immigrant mothers away from their children
By claiming that an excess of compassion is in fact a social blight, Saad’s book and others offer a theoretical framework for selfishness

G iven just how influential Saad’s book has become among people with power and political capital, such as Elon Musk , the billionaire investor Marc Andreessen , and the billionaire hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman , I decided to read it myself

This was not idle curiosity: These arguments plainly matter, and they have serious implications for American politics. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: The conservative attack on empathy ] By empathy , Saad means “a noble and evolutionarily selected virtue, a central feature of our humanity” which, he says, is correlated with kindness

What he means by suicidal is less clearly defined, but the overarching idea is that when people—typically woke liberals—advocate certain actions or policy positions out of empathy for other people, rather than based on Saad’s idea of objective reasoning, they undermine the societal values of security and cohesion

To illustrate this concept, Saad nods, in his introduction, to policies that elevate the needs of an allegedly oppressed minority over those of everyone else, such as efforts to raise immigration rates or to allow transgender women to compete in women’s sports
For Saad, these policies are not pet peeves, but catastrophes with civilizational consequences
The book is loosely constructed, with chapters that leap wildly from subject to subject—from how to punish criminals guilty of rape and murder to Canadian tax policy
This messiness reflects the shambolic nature of the underlying argument
Interspersed throughout are angry accounts from Saad’s own life, in which his critics always happen to suffer from misguided empathy

This was ostensibly the problem that afflicted Saad’s interviewer for an academic job, who took issue with a video Saad had posted on social media in which he called a woman who littered on the beach a “human pig.” Two attendees of a talk Saad gave, who took issue with his stated claim that all men are potential pedophiles, were also apparently guilty of forsaking objective reasoning for emotional impulse
As a category, suicidal empathy is almost infinitely capacious

Saad’s examples include lax immigration laws; high taxes; mandatory sensitivity training; universal health care; “the diversity, inclusion, and equity cult”; every manifestation of anti-Zionism; “twerking drag queens during kindergarten reading hour”; and “communism, socialism, and the welfare and nanny states.” He also offers anecdotes about people who suffered for their empathy, such as the researchers Zaida Catalan and Michael Sharp, who were killed by locals in the Democratic Republic of Congo while they were on a mission to investigate human-rights violations there

Saad offers up this case study with a haughty tone and the following observation: “At times, people place themselves in harm’s way in their noble desire to help others.” I had to pause and read that sentence twice
What Saad meant as a warning against empathy struck me as evidence that human beings are capable of great acts of heroic moral character
In my religious tradition—Catholicism, just like Bishop Barron’s—self-sacrifice represents the apex of love and humility, epitomized by the Crucifixion of Jesus and the lives of many saints
The concept of forgiving those who have wronged us is essential in Christianity, which led me to wonder what Barron and other prominent Christians see in a theory like Saad’s
T o the degree that books such as Saad’s are meant to help conservatives resolve their internal conflicts and ignore their consciences, they are basically right-wing self-help guides
Stuckey’s Toxic Empathy seems especially targeted at conservative Christians who feel torn about subjects such as immigration and welfare
Stuckey is at pains to reassure her readers that any dissonance they might feel between their religious duties and political interests is a treacherous mirage generated by the left

The goal of “toxic empathy,” she says, is “to get us to suppress our opposition to a particular issue or point of view by playing upon our desire to be a good person.” By this account, liberals are emotionally exploiting feelings of guilt or shame in conservatives to persuade them to support left-wing goals
And, like much self-help literature, the anti-empathy genre does not have to make sense to change minds

In Saad’s imagination, seemingly any personal or political cost, such as paying high taxes, or halting human encroachment on the habitat of endangered animals, is a form of individual or collective suicide

Attentive readers will note that the literal costs of these actions fall well short of death, but making every issue sound ruinous is important for conservatives who wish to believe that their at-times harsh policies—such as denying poor people health insurance—are somehow morally necessary to preserve themselves and, indeed, all of Western civilization. [ Hillary Rodham Clinton: MAGA’s war on empathy ] In theory, Saad is describing the putative destruction of traditional Western culture by liberals and immigrants, through either the great replacement of white Christians or a grand shift in public opinion

But given Saad’s choice of targets, what this idea means in practice is that every time you pay your taxes, sit through a diversity-training session at work, or interact with a disabled employee at the post office, you are witnessing the collapse of the West
To help burnish this point, Saad contorts progressive thinking so that it conforms to his rigid views

He dismisses leftists who approach homelessness as a housing-affordability problem as somehow blinkered by their misguided empathy. “Progressive policies presume that it is compassionate to ignore the fact that homelessness is in large part due to mental disease and substance addiction,” he writes. “It is perhaps more empathetic, albeit incorrect, to blame greedy capitalist landlords for the lack of affordable housing.” Saad is plainly unmoved by the fact that the median price of single-family homes in the United States is now five times that of the median annual income

title: Wait, what are the rules around cellphone etiquette now?
excerpt: Recently, while taking the metro to work, I encountered something that shocked me
body: Recently, while taking the metro to work, I encountered something that shocked me
The train was pulling up, just as the man in front of me tapped to pay to go through the gate, and a woman pushed past me to cut me in line
I still made the train (after I briefly considered acting in a way that would have made us both late for work), but as I passed each stop I got angrier and angrier

Why did she think her commute was more important than someone else’s? We learn to wait our turn when we’re children — why was that lesson lost all these years later?  I’m not the only one irritated by this kind of thing
Almost half of Americans say that they’ve noticed people are ruder in the wake of the Covid pandemic

Whether it’s poor behavior at the airport or blasting music from your phone with no headphones in public, it’s like people don’t know how to act anymore.  Kirsty Sedgman is a professor at the University of Bristol and the author of the book On Being Unreasonable: Breaking the Rules and Making Things Better

She argues that while people might not mind them as much anymore, manners are important.  “They encourage us to think about others and to behave in ways that are not antisocial and potentially even dangerous,” she told Vox. “How can we have these conversations so that we figure out what we all want social life and public space to be like in a way that benefits everybody and doesn’t accidentally exclude [anyone]? While some etiquette rules are pretty self explanatory (let’s not cut in line!), others are more difficult to navigate. “I always try to make a point and I’m not perfect, believe me,” Sedgman said. “I’m not saying that I know how to behave in every single circumstance and I’m always right
I’m no Emily Post.” Post was the socialite who literally wrote the book on the subject: Etiquette in Society, in Business, in Politics and at Home was first published in the 1920s
More than a century later, her family is still in the business of teaching us how to mind our manners
Lizzie Post is Emily Post’s great-great granddaughter and co-president of the Emily Post Institute
That’s a title and pedigree that could come with a lot of pressure

But Post says it’s all about your audience. “A lot of times, as long as I don’t get the sense that they would prefer a very formalized version of me, I try to reassure people: laugh, joke, swear, it’s okay,” Post said
Audience isn’t the only thing that’s changed — the times have too
How has etiquette shifted over the years? And how do we navigate newer things — like our phones? We find out that and more on this week’s episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Post, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545
For a long time etiquette has just been something that’s agreed upon
You have to have certain manners to socialize in certain circles and within certain classes
Why do you think that’s happened? My great-great-grandmother wrote from 1922 to 1960
While she talked about the standards of the day, she also allowed those standards to change
Think about 1922 to 1960 — there were huge swings in how people behaved
Chaperones were gone from the book by her second edition
Life was changing and evolving and she changed and evolved with it.  Etiquette is a French word — it sounds fancy
I think that it can very easily have these connotations of being something that is about a secret society, or it’s only about formality, or it’s only for people who are very wealthy

It can also start to feel a lot like judgment.  One of the reasons etiquette can feel so out of sorts, particularly right now, is because times are changing and they’re just changing really quickly.  I think phone etiquette is really, really emblematic of that
One thing that is so common is people playing music or having their phone on speaker, no headphones

Do we just not know how to act when it comes to our phones?  There are definitely rules of courtesy and blaring anything out of your phone, whether it’s a phone call, it’s a FaceTime call, it’s your TikTok feed, or that movie that you’re watching, is all inappropriate when other people are a captive audience and haven’t asked to be.  It’s this mindful moment where people forget where they are

They’re so used to being in their own world with their phone six inches from their face that they forget that anyone can even hear what it is that they’re doing on their phone at that particular moment.  It’s really hard to correct this behavior because generally, we don’t correct other people’s behaviors
I admit, especially in public spaces, I am Team Mind My Business

But at what point do you step in? It’s a really tough judgment call, and it’s going to be different for every situation.  I think that when I am in a space that I’m only going to occupy for a short time, I am telling myself, “Mind my own business, don’t worry about it.” When it’s that train ride that we’re starting, or that four-hour flight that you’re on, I think we start to have to say something and to ask, “Hey, could you put some headphones on while you’re enjoying that or watching that or on your call?”  I say, “Could you,” because they might not have headphones with them, but even if they don’t, it’s a reminder
It’s like that check of awareness that, “Oh, this thing I’m doing is impacting people around me.” Here’s the rub: You can’t control other people’s behavior
You cannot control if this person is going to get defensive
If you’re going to ask the question, be prepared for rudeness in return
And I hate saying that, but it is the reality
We can’t control other people’s behavior
So there’s clearly a wrong way to use speakerphone and FaceTime
What’s the right way to use them?  We do a lot of talking on our speakerphones, even in our own homes

You might be moving from one room to another, passing through the living room where people are watching TV or you’re in the kitchen and all of a sudden a roommate has come into the room while you’re on a call that’s on speakerphone
You really want to let the person on the other end of the phone know that there’s other people present now.  My cousin is so good about this

title: This weather threat costs us billions. And it’s about to get worse.
excerpt: Kevin Ross removes damaged vinyl sheets from underneath his sister's mobile home in Watkins, Colorado
body: Kevin Ross removes damaged vinyl sheets from underneath his sister's mobile home in Watkins, Colorado

The trailer park was heavily damaged by hail and very strong winds. | Denver Post/Getty Images This story was originally published by High Country News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk Collaboration

At a specialized cold lab in Boulder, Colorado, where indoor temperatures hover around minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 20 degrees Celsius), atmospheric researcher Anthony Bernal Ayala slices hailstones with a band saw, revealing layers of icy growth like the rings of a tree

These frozen rings — clear or cloudy, thick or thin — indicate the conditions in which the hail formed: A clear layer signals the water froze slowly, while a cloudy layer means it happened quickly, trapping air bubbles

Bernal Ayala then analyzes the crystalline structures, particles, and isotopes preserved in these layers. “All that information can tell you a wonderful story of how the hailstone was growing, but nobody — not until now — was able to tap into that history,” said Bernal Ayala, who works for Atmospheric and Environmental Research, part of the JANUS Research Group
Bernal Ayala’s research, conducted at the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), is part of a historic effort to study one of the costliest weather hazards
Researchers hope their findings will help protect lives and property from the stones that careen to Earth, battering roofs, pummeling crops, and pockmarking cars

From 2023 to 2025, annual severe thunderstorm losses exceeded $50 billion nationwide, according to the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety — more than double the losses seen just a decade earlier
Hail accounted for 60 percent to 80 percent of the damage
In Colorado, one of the country’s most hail-prone states, hail — not wildfire — is the main factor driving up insurance premiums
And researchers expect larger, more damaging hailstones to become more common with climate change. “It’s going to just keep getting costlier and costlier,” Bernal Ayala said
Even basic questions about hail have been notoriously hard to study

But a long-awaited resurgence in research, including the first major US field campaign to study hail in more than 40 years, could help change that.  ICECHIP — the “In-situ Collaborative Experiment for the Collection of Hail In the Plains” — aims to improve forecasts, make warnings more precise and help communities better prepare

It received $11 million in funding from the National Science Foundation in 2024, just before deep cuts hit the foundation in 2025.  For six weeks in spring 2025, about 100 scientists and university students chased hailstorms across the Central Plains and Front Range, from the Canadian to the Mexican border, using radar trucks to track storms and drones to take aerial footage

Researchers photographed hail with high-speed cameras, measured its impact with a tool called a disdrometer, recorded hail’s distribution and size based on its imprints on foam pads, captured it in specialized funnels, and crushed it to test its strength.  Scientists from the Australian Bureau of Meteorology also used balloons to release golf ball-sized sensors into storms

Once aloft, each hail-like probe collected data on how fast it was traveling and whether ice was growing on it; a microphone even recorded water droplets and hailstones hitting it. “This has really been the first time where we’ve been able to do a real comprehensive look at hail on the ground, hail aloft, the storm itself, the environment around the storm — just everything all at once,” said Becky Adams-Selin, ICECHIP’s lead investigator and a principal scientist at Atmospheric and Environmental Research, JANUS Research Group.  ICECHIP’s samples were packed into 26 cooler-sized boxes and brought to NCAR
This internationally renowned hub for weather and climate research has been used to study hail for decades

In one of its last major campaigns, in the 1970s, the US investigated Soviet claims that it could suppress hail.  Researchers say there’s no other US lab like it; the backup plan to store ICECHIP’s samples involved using a walk-in freezer from a fast-food restaurant
Now NCAR’s own future is uncertain: In late 2025, the Trump administration said it would dissolve the center and transfer its work out of state

The University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR), which manages NCAR, sued the administration in March, alleging that it’s targeting NCAR to punish Colorado for retaining its mail-in voting system and because Gov
Jared Polis initially refused to release former Mesa County clerk Tina Peters, a 2020 election denier imprisoned for breaching election security and undermining election integrity
In June, a federal judge temporarily blocked the White House from dismantling NCAR

The government has until Sept. 30 to respond to the lawsuit. “I can’t even quantify the impact that it would have to our community if we lost NCAR,” Victor Gensini, professor of meteorology at Northern Illinois University, told HCN. “They are the beating heart.” Previous research has predicted climate change’s effects on hail, noting that warmer temperatures could melt smaller hailstones before they land but also fuel stronger updrafts, keeping hailstones airborne longer and allowing them to grow bigger, enabling the most damaging hail to become more common.  A record-setting stone recovered in Yuma County, Colorado, in 2023 measured more than 5 inches across
That year, the state logged 176 reports of hail 2 inches or greater, surpassing the previous record of 91 reports in 2018, according to the Colorado Climate Center
Scientists say it’s difficult to know how much of the rise in damage is due to the increase in large hail versus the increased development in hail hotspots

The connection between a rapidly growing human footprint and higher insured losses has been dubbed the “expanding bull’s-eye effect.” Gensini, a principal ICECHIP investigator, cites the development boom east of the Front Range, along Colorado’s Interstate 25 corridor, which has grown explosively in recent decades
The population of the Fort Collins metro area alone has doubled since 1990 to around 375,000 residents, according to the US Census Bureau

This is happening across the Western US, as previously rural or open areas become densely populated, increasingly expensive targets for hail. “Colorado is the poster child for what I expect the next 25 years to look like for hail,” Gensini said
In 2019, Fort Collins became one of the first cities to adopt hail-specific roofing requirements for new builds and remodels
Marcus Coldiron, the city’s chief building official, said it was partly in response to all the shingles and roofing materials taken to the landfill after a catastrophic hailstorm in 2018
It’s still unclear how well the requirements are working: Coldiron said fewer permits were being issued for roof replacements and fewer shingles were going to the dump
However, Fort Collins also hasn’t experienced a hailstorm as devastating as the one that hit in 2018

A growing number of Front Range communities now require impact-resistant shingles in their building codes, and Colorado legislators recently passed a law offering grants to residents who install more resilient roofing

ICECHIP’s researchers are also investigating how they can improve building materials as billion-dollar losses from single storms become more common. “The dollars are simply piling up so fast,” said Ian Giammanco, a lead research meteorologist at the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety, one of ICECHIP’s key partners. “We’re still trying to understand how do we get the best materials onto roofs, onto people’s homes, onto businesses to actually start shaving off these losses.”

title: Why Democrats stopped talking about climate
excerpt: Michigan Democratic congressional candidate Will Lawrence speaks with reporters on September 14, 2026, in Mason, Michigan. | Nic Antaya/Getty Images William Law
body: Michigan Democratic congressional candidate Will Lawrence speaks with reporters on September 14, 2026, in Mason, Michigan. | Nic Antaya/Getty Images William Lawrence is a Democrat running to represent Michigan’s Lansing-area Seventh Congressional District with a campaign that largely focuses on data centers and affordability

It’s not an unusual story in 2026 — but not long ago, Lawrence was cutting his teeth in progressive politics as a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, primarily focused on organizing around the climate crisis

His arc, from progressive activist to politician, is emblematic of a bigger trend, as a wave of millennial progressives in midterm races across the country try to lean into issues that have broader, more immediate appeal with voters
But that arc also raises big questions about the left’s changing priorities

In a recent interview for Vox’s podcast and video series America, Actually , host Astead Herndon spoke with Lawrence about his past activism and how he has pivoted. “It can sometimes feel like…folks hop from issue to issue, whether it’s climate, even anti-AI right now, without those things being solved,” Herndon told Lawrence
According to Lawrence, “that’s the reality of the time

It seems like everything is unraveling, and it is because the whole social, economic, political compact is being renegotiated, not just in this country, but on a global stage.” Still, Lawrence said, that earlier organizing shapes how he sees different challenges today

The two also discussed whether opposition to data centers and AI has wide, regular-voter appeal in places like Michigan and how Lawrence went from hopeless and disengaged to regaining a sense of agency through organizing
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel

You started in Sunrise and were at the forefront of a young progressive movement that was aligned at that time — in 2018, 2019, and I think still — with progressive members of Congress like Rashida Tlaib or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
I remember reporting about Sunrise at the time
The goal was to elect a Bernie Sanders, but the other goal was to have the party largely embrace things like a Green New Deal
How would you grade the efforts of the climate movement of that time, looking back? I think we did some things very well
We put climate jobs and justice at the top of the agenda for the incoming Biden administration
I think the Bernie-Biden task force is an often overlooked but very important chapter of that whole story, where Bernie and Biden both understood they had to bring their people to the table
And that’s how Build Back Better got negotiated
We fought hard for Build Back Better , and ultimately came up two votes shy in the United States Senate

Do you see that as a success or a failure of the climate movement? I think Build Back Better was a success in coming to the table and negotiating, from the Green New Deal to Build Back Better, and then what we ended up with was the Inflation Reduction Act after it passed the final filter, which was Sen
At the time, now, how I felt about it was, this is historic
This is the largest investment in green jobs and infrastructure in United States history
I’m tremendously proud of the work that I did and so many others did
Just in my district alone, we’ve delivered $26 billion in investment for manufacturing and sustainability because of the Inflation Reduction Act
But at the time, we knew that this is maybe 5 percent or 10 percent of what we need in scope
And now we’re experiencing the consequences of that
Obviously, we still have a very volatile economy
We still lack energy security because we now have closed the Strait of Hormuz
We’re still too dependent on a global oil market, and we could use many more investments in solar and other kinds of renewable energy than we have now
And ultimately, it wasn’t enough for the Biden-Harris administration to be able to win reelection, because people didn’t feel it enough in their pocketbooks
Why do you think Democrats are talking less about climate? I think it’s the intensity of the crises that we face

It feels like we’re falling through midair, after the end of all of the constitutional protections, the rule of law, and the economic security that people had previously enjoyed.  There are a lot of very acute and urgent crises, and I think that that has bumped climate, which is a super massive but also somewhat slow-moving crisis, a little bit lower on the priority list just in terms of what comes up for people on the Hill
You went back to Michigan to focus on housing and advocacy

Did that make you think a little differently about the national work you were doing? I think it’s fair to say that when I was younger, I got very focused on this climate issue, and I was very focused on it because it is this existential crisis we all face
But it was after the pandemic that I wanted to bring my work closer to home
I wanted to do the work of putting down roots in the place that had raised me and make my life there

And in seeking to organize there, it was clear that we needed an in to organize that was more immediate. “I believe in the agency of regular people taking charge of our own lives and working together to build a better future.” More immediate than the Green New Deal
Than the Green New Deal or than the looming climate crisis

People know that that’s an issue, but they’re like, “I’ve gotta pay rent at the end of the month.” And as an organizer, I believe that you have to listen to people, you have to hear what’s going on for them, and then work on issues that have the potential to bring people together
Whether you’re in the city of Lansing, whether you’re in small towns, urban, rural, suburban, young or old, everybody can agree that the rent is too damn high and it’s too hard to buy a home anymore
Were you surprised Trump won the state in 2024?  No

title: Inside a quest to learn about the ocean’s mysterious “deep reefs”
excerpt: An autonomous reef monitoring structure (ARMS) in the mesophotic zone. | © Luiz Rocha This story was originally published in  The Highlight
body: An autonomous reef monitoring structure (ARMS) in the mesophotic zone. | © Luiz Rocha This story was originally published in  The Highlight
To get access to member-exclusive stories like this every month,  become a Vox Member today
PALAU, Micronesia — On a bright, sunny day last May, I stood on a boat surrounded by the turquoise waters of the island nation of Palau
I was there in the western Pacific watching scuba divers as they prepared to bring up evidence of a mysterious aquatic world.  Palau is famous for its spectacular and rich coral reefs

But these divers were planning to descend past those sun-lit marine communities and down into a lesser-known twilight zone known as the “mesophotic coral ecosystems.”  Mesophotic essentially means “middle” and “light,” which is where these ecosystems are — not quite in the bright daylight, not quite in the profound darkness, but somewhere in between

For simplicity’s sake, we’ll call these communities, which range from some 30 meters to 150 meters below the surface, the “deep reefs.”  One of the divers on the boat with me was a zoologist and curator at the California Academy of Sciences named Luiz Rocha, who has spent decades studying these deep reefs and their secrets.  “Anything between 30 meters and 150 meters is really, really unknown,” he told me
Because these deep reefs are so unknown, researchers like Rocha are left with big questions

They want to get a baseline picture of what is going on in these ecosystems — even just who lives there! — so that they can better understand how they function.  They’ve also tried to work out whether ( or not ) these deep reefs might provide a refuge for species living in shallower coral reefs

I was in Palau for Vox’s Unexplainable podcast because, in an effort to gather more information about these mysterious places, Rocha left some scientific structures down in these twilight depths back in 2016
Those structures then spent almost a decade becoming encrusted with all kinds of marine life

And now, Rocha was back to retrieve them, hoping that he — along with many other scientists — would be able to open them up, like a box of scientific puzzle pieces, full of clues about this under-understood marine world

View Link So what is a mesophotic “deep reef”?  One thing that’s often acknowledged in papers about and descriptions of the “mesophotic coral ecosystems” is that scientists don’t know as much as they’d like to. A National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration article about them from 2019 is full of “may’s” as in: they may “serve as essential fish habitat for economically and ecologically important species.” Researchers do know some things, of course

They know that these deep reefs can be found in many of the same locations as shallower coral reefs — so mainly the tropical and subtropical parts of the world, like Micronesia , the Caribbean , and even the Gulf of Mexico
They’ve found that there are many species that seem to be unique to these places, and recent research points to their potential susceptibility to climate change
Researchers have also gotten a sense of some of the key differences between these deep reefs and their shallower coral neighbors
In shallow reefs, hard corals team up with photosynthesizing algaes

The algaes provide the corals with nutrients, and the corals secrete a calcium-carbonate matrix that helps create the architecture of the reef.  As you go deeper, though, the light begins to fade, and the opportunities for photosynthesis start to fade with it
So the animals living down in the deep reefs are the ones that can survive in a dimmer, cooler world

Why are these places so mysterious?  Scientists can dive into the deep reefs to try to learn more about these understudied places — as Rocha has — but exploring down at 100 meters requires more difficult, riskier technical diving than exploring at shallower depths

The deeper you dive, for example, the faster gasses get pushed into your tissues, which imposes limits on these really deep dives. “We have a very, very short time,” Rocha says, “And by short time, I mean five minutes

Six, seven minutes.”  Scientists might take some pictures in that time, or make some measurements, or collect a few samples, but then they have to move back upwards, a process which can take hours because they have to rise slowly to avoid decompression sickness
It is, obviously, not particularly efficient to study an ecosystem in five- to seven-minute bursts

People have also used remote operated vehicles and submersibles to explore the deep reefs, but those have their own issues, and cameras can’t always capture all the detail you might want, or photograph more secretive, cryptic animals

So huge gaps remain in scientific knowledge about these ecosystems.  “Whenever we go somewhere,” Rocha says, “the first thing we find is new species. … It’s the most basic thing in science you can do.” But this effort goes beyond just cataloguing new species of fish or sponges or sea slugs.  Rocha wants to answer seemingly fundamental questions like: What is the main energy source for everything down here in the dimmer light? What does the food chain look like? How have things evolved to live down at these depths? How similar are they to the shallow ecosystems, and how different? How are they affected by climate change — and what’s the most efficient way to protect them?  But, “in some ways we don’t even know what questions to ask,” Rocha says. “We really only know what questions to ask after we have a baseline understanding of what the ecosystem is

And for deep reefs, we don’t know that yet.”  A new way to understand the deep reefs using “prefab housing” Rocha is not deterred by the enormous number of question marks that surround these deep reefs

For years now, he has been gathering bits of basic information about them, often via those very short dives.  About a decade ago, though, Rocha got interested in another method for sampling the biodiversity of this sort of marine ecosystem — a technique involving “ autonomous reef monitoring structures ” (ARMS)
Basically, each ARMS is a stack of several PVC plates, separated at uniform intervals and attached to a base plate
They look like little grey, featureless hotels

You take them to a place that you want to study, bring them down, secure them, and then leave them alone for a while to let them collect…life. “As soon as you drop any kind of clean structure on a reef,” Rocha says, “it starts getting colonized by larvae of everything around it — of sponges, gorgonians, corals

And then, because there’s all a lot of hiding spots between the plates — so between the floors of the hotel — they start getting colonized by shrimp, by mollusks, by ascidians, by anything you can imagine in the ocean. … And it becomes this stable, diverse mini reef, if you will, packed with a lot of biodiversity that would be very hard to collect all at once in any given reef.” A few years after that initial drop, you come back, collect the ARMS, and then study the mini reef that has grown on them
You can sample and touch and analyze things to your heart’s content.  It’s not only a very effective way to collect lots of creatures, all at once, but also a great way to do so in a standardized way

If you went down — or sent a robot down — to collect an encrusted rock from a reef, you could learn a lot about the life on it, but it would be hard to compare the life on that rock to life on other rocks from other reefs, or even the same reef, because each rock would have its own unique characteristics

Not so for ARMS. “ Every one’s the same,” Chris Meyer, director of the Smithsonian Global ARMS program, told me, “It’s prefab housing, and then you just look to see who moves in.”  To Rocha, this seemed like a great way to get a really good, long look at the deep reefs instead of the brief glimpses he was getting from diving
It was also, he told me, fairly cheap to deploy them
So from 2016 to 2018, with some private funding, he and his colleagues left ARMS in some of the deep reefs around Palau — as well as in Guam, the Marshall Islands, and French Polynesia

They installed some around 50 meters, and some around 100, and then some around 10 meters, so he could compare the deep reefs to their shallower neighbors.  After that, he waited.  In fact, he waited a little longer than he would have liked, because the retrieval of ARMS is more expensive than deploying them, so he had to work out more funding.  Eventually, private funders agreed to underwrite the retrieval of the ARMS that Rocha had left
Which is how he and his fellow divers finally found themselves on a boat in Palau again, ready to pull up these structures for the deep
Opening the scientific puzzle box Over the course of a few days, I watched a whole team of people pull several ARMS out of the deep reefs of Palau
Some of the ARMS were relatively sparse, but others were almost fuzzy with organisms — vibrant with red and orange and green and pink and white
One had a massive sponge attached to it, another had several delicate fronds dangling from it like coralline ferns

The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved lie detector, according to a Department of Defense budget request

The program, called “Polygraph+” or “Polygraph Next,” will focus on scoring algorithms that use AI and machine learning, as well as a technique called “standoff sensing,” which can take physiological readings from a person without attaching a device to them
The project aims to improve the accuracy and reliability of polygraph assessments
But it could just be the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies

Here’s how the program could work—and why experts say AI-enabled lie detection is “the worst of both worlds.” —Amit Katwala Young organs may not be a fountain of youth for recipients Around this time last year, a hot mic caught Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping discussing the possibility of living forever . “With the developments of biotechnology, human organs can be continuously transplanted, and people can live younger and younger, and even achieve immortality,” Putin reportedly said
He seemed to be referring to the “replacement” theory of longevity, supported by experiments that involved physically stitching young mice to old ones
Unfortunately for Putin, new research on transplanted hearts pours a little cold water on this idea

The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning and on a technique called “standoff sensing,” which refers to the ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to a subject’s person

According to details of the budget document, which were first reported by Inside Defense , the project will “modernize federal polygraph and credibility assessment technologies” to improve their accuracy and reliability

But the project may be just the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies. “It’s a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” says Kyri Kotsoglou, a legal scholar at Northumbria University in the UK who studies the use of polygraphs in the justice system
The move comes at a time of high tension within the department
Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has been increasingly turning to polygraph tests in an attempt to find the sources of alleged leaks to the press

In September, the New York Times reported that around 50 officers on the Joint Staff had been given polygraph tests after news coverage reported on the depletion of US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.  Polygraph+ will be run by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which conducts background checks for the federal government

According to the budget document, which has not yet been approved by Congress, the new technology will be used for vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” It is not yet clear which specific technologies will be used, and the DCSA did not respond to a request for more information.  But other Pentagon efforts offer potential clues
In 2023, the department’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) ran an open submission process to find companies with products that could be used for deception detection

It selected two companies to build prototypes : Presage Technologies, which claims to be able to measure heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras, and Altec Research, a medical sensor company now branching out into non-contact sensing technologies
A screenshot of Altec’s prototype technology released by the DIU shows that it tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity
Presage Technologies and Altec Research did not respond to requests for comment
The DIU declined to comment.  Altec Research has built a prototype that tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity
ALTEC RESEARCH Current lie detection technology has barely changed since the polygraph was invented in the 1920s
Examiners rely on blood pressure, pulse, breathing, and sweat measurements to determine if someone is lying

They make judgments about the veracity of respondents’ replies on the basis of differences in their physiological response to baseline questions like “Is the sky blue?” and target questions like “Have you ever committed a crime?” The federal government conducts tens of thousands of the tests each year while screening employees, but the reliability of this technology has been repeatedly challenged—and its results are rarely admissible in court

In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment concluded that there was very limited evidence supporting the polygraph’s use for screening employees, and in 2003 , the US National Research Council (NRC) said evidence for its efficacy was “weak at best.”  Research suggests humans can spot a lie just over half the time without any technical assistance
The American Polygraph Association claims the polygraph is between 80% and 94% accurate
But the 2003 NRC report pointed out that a screening test with this level of accuracy could still lead to a lot of mistakes
The DOD employs 2.8 million people; an imperfect system applied at that scale could end up falsely accusing tens of thousands
Polygraph interpretations are often subjective: Different examiners get wildly different results , and people from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive

What’s more, with training it’s possible for interviewees to learn a variety of countermeasures that can help beat the test; for example, they may artificially heighten their physiological response to baseline questions by stepping on a pin hidden in their shoe.  “If you know how it works, you can beat it,” says Sophie van der Zee, an associate professor who studies deception at Erasmus University in Rotterdam
She says the machine’s biggest effect is deterrence—often, subjects confess before it even begins. “But that only works if people think a polygraph works,” she points out
Various new strategies for lie detection have been attempted over the decades , with technologies ranging from thermal cameras to pupil trackers to brain scans
None of them have yielded reliable results outside the lab

The problem is that there’s no single telltale sign of lying that’s true for everyone all the time. “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose,” says van der Zee.  AI could theoretically improve polygraphs if it could find patterns in the data that examiners can’t
AI algorithms are also more likely to be used for “multi-modal” deception detection, which seeks to combine multiple measurements into an overall deception “score” that is harder for people to game

Three things are happening under the surface that lie detection tries to home in on, van der Zee says: physiological stress, cognitive load, and the conscious efforts people make to conceal the fact that they’re lying
Current polygraph technology tackles only one. “The more you can have combined methods that approach it from these three different angles, the more successful you will be,” van der Zee says
This isn’t a new concept—in the 2000s, researchers at Manchester Metropolitan University in the UK developed a system called Silent Talker that generated a deception score from video footage
This was later folded into iBorderCtrl, an EU-funded pilot program
In the US, a project called AVATAR incorporated eye tracking, voice analysis, and body movement detection into a tool for use at border crossings
All these projects have quietly faded away.  Kotsoglou says combining AI and the polygraph is “the worst of both worlds” because it adds uncertainty on top of invalidity

Even if AI or machine learning can spot previously unseen patterns in physiological data, it won’t be able to reliably link them to lying because there is no real ground truth.  “Even if you have all the records in the world from polygraph tests, you don’t know whether those polygraph tests are right or not,” says Marion Oswald, a professor of law who has written with Kotsoglou on the use of polygraphs in the justice system

She fears that new forms of lie detection will, like the polygraph, be used more as a psychological prop than a scientific tool.  “It seems very much a response to the concern of the current administration to leaks and perceived lack of loyalty,” says Oswald. “[Lie detection is] being used as a threat, to intimidate and force people to confess to things, as opposed to anything that’s actually getting valid information.”

title: Young organs may not be a fountain of youth for recipients
excerpt: Young hearts don't stay young for long: New research shows that transplanted hearts quickly take on the biological age of whoever receives them — meaning a
body: Young hearts don't stay young for long: New research shows that transplanted hearts quickly take on the biological age of whoever receives them — meaning a 30-year-old heart given to a 70-year-old recipient will soon "act" 70

The body's environment calls the shots: Researchers found that neither the recipient's blood nor other organs were meaningfully affected by the donor heart's age, suggesting the body's broader environment overpowers any rejuvenating potential a young organ might carry

A silver lining for transplant medicine: The findings could push surgeons to stop discarding older donor hearts, since biological age appears to reset after transplant anyway — potentially expanding a critically short supply of viable organs

Immortality remains out of reach: The study underscores just how stubbornly complex aging is — reversing it entirely would require unwinding DNA damage, structural decay, and cellular wear across every tissue simultaneously, which scientists say is an enormous, likely impossible, challenge. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145083" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Around this time last year I was attending an aging conference in Manchester, listening to a talk about fly aging, when my phone started pinging

News outlets were reporting that a hot mic had caught Russia’s and China’s leaders discussing the possibility of living forever . “With the developments of biotechnology, human organs can be continuously transplanted, and people can live younger and younger, and even achieve immortality,” Russia’s Vladimir Putin reportedly told China’s Xi Jinping
He seems to have been referring to the “replacement” theory of longevity, which has been supported by multiple experiments that involved physically stitching young mice to old ones
Something about the young blood rejuvenated the old mice
Perhaps young organs could rejuvenate world leaders in their 70s, too
Unfortunately for Putin, new research pours a little cold water on this idea
Studies on transplanted hearts in both mice and humans suggest that new hearts soon adopt the biological age of the recipient, no matter how young they were to begin with
The finding could be important for transplantation, but it also highlights just how complex aging—and rejuvenation—are
Jesse Poganik at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston is one of the many scientists trying to understand exactly what it is about the bodies of young mice that rejuvenates old ones
Plenty of research has focused on seeking the secrets of youth in young blood
But what if it’s something about young organs instead? To find out, he and his colleagues performed a set of heart transplants in mice

In humans, heart transplants typically involve removing a damaged or injured heart and replacing it with another from a donor who is usually much younger than the recipient. (When Poganik assessed hospital records, he found that most recipients were about 20 years older than their donors.) The mouse transplants were different: Mice received a second heart, implanted in the neck—a procedure that’s slightly simpler and allows scientists to compare the new hearts with the existing ones
In some cases, young adult mice were given a heart from a middle-aged donor
In others, middle-aged mice got young hearts
The team used a trio of “aging clocks” —molecular tools used to estimate the biological ages of tissues and whole organisms—to assess whether the additional hearts affected the mice in any way
These clocks were good at predicting the chronological age of mice that didn’t get new hearts
Poganik says he was expecting to see a reciprocal effect, and that young hearts might benefit older animals, for example
In previous work by other members of his team, young mice that got old hearts experienced a buildup of senescent cells in their other organs
These cells are thought to contribute to the aging process, suggesting that receiving an old organ might prematurely age an animal
When he and his colleagues analyzed the transplanted hearts between four and six months after surgery, they found that the hearts seemed to have adopted the biological age of the recipients
Young hearts got older, and old hearts got younger. “The environment of the transplanted organ really dictates how it seems to behave biologically,” he says
The findings were published online at bioRxiv last week

The team also looked at each mouse’s blood and other organs—including its original heart—and were surprised to find that they seemed to be unaffected by the presence of the new heart, despite the age of its donor
The finding was backed up by data from human heart transplants
People who receive a donor heart must typically undergo a series of heart biopsies after surgery
The tiny pieces of heart tissue collected from people who had heart transplants at Brigham and Women’s have been stored for decades

And when Poganik and his colleagues tested their biological ages with the aging clocks, they found a similar pattern: No matter the age of the donor, a new heart quickly adopts the biological age of the person who received it

It’s not clear why this is, but João Pedro de Magalhães, who studies aging at the University of Birmingham in the UK and was not involved in the study, thinks it might have something to do with the recipient’s immune system
Perhaps immune cells circulating in the blood might affect markers of aging in the new organ, he says
Perhaps the potential rejuvenating effects of a young heart end up being diluted by all the other aged components of an older body, Poganik suggests
Or maybe a single organ just isn’t enough to see an effect

Poganik hopes his finding will encourage surgeons to consider using hearts from older donors, many of which are discarded on the assumption they won’t function as well. (Machines used to preserve organs before transplantation are changing that already—and Poganik has worked on another study showing that these devices seem to rejuvenate donor livers to some extent.) But the study also highlights just how complicated aging is

If organs seem to be getting older by one measure but not by another, how can we get a full picture of the biological age of an organ, or a person? This complexity means that scientists are not likely to discover a true way to completely reverse aging, says Poganik. “That would mean that every aspect of aging has to go back in time,” he says

Reversing DNA damage, structural damage, and all the other degradations that are part of the aging package, across all our various cells and tissues, presents an enormous challenge. “There are aspects of biological age that are probably reversible, and there are aspects that are probably not,” he says
This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter

title: In ‘NAZA,’ Israeli whistleblowers’ revelations about civilian deaths in Gaza reflect a longer history of Palestinian isolation
