<title>In ‘NAZA,’ Israeli whistleblowers’ revelations about civilian deaths in Gaza reflect a longer history of Palestinian isolation</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762096/original/file-20260924-60-i55q85.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8256%2C5504&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">&#39;NAZA&#39; filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor conducted interviews with anonymous members of Israeli military and intelligence services from the rooftops of Tel Aviv, Israel.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/general-view-shows-the-israeli-city-of-tel-aviv-on-august-news-photo/2165972971?adppopup=true">Gil Cohen-Magen/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>There’s a powerful scene in Moroccan-French-Israeli filmmaker Simone Bitton’s 2004 documentary “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0413018/">Wall</a>,” which tells the story of the construction of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/08865655.2016.1174601">the West Bank barrier</a>, a 448-mile – or 721-kilometer – network of walls and fences dividing large parts of the West Bank from Israel.</p>

<p>A concrete slab is slowly lowered into place in order to complete a section of the wall. Inch by inch, the vibrant, hilly Palestinian community on the other side gets smaller and smaller. </p>

<p>And then – just like that – a world that’s a stone’s throw away is gone. </p>

<p><a href="https://edinburghuniversitypress.com/book-israel-palestine.html">As someone</a> <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/arrested-movement-in-the-middle-east-9780755656721/">who studies</a> the restrictions placed on Palestinians, I often think about this scene as a microcosm of Israel’s decades-long use of walls, checkpoints and surveillance technologies to seal off Palestinians from the rest of society.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A huge slab of concrete approaches another slab with a small opening of the community on the other side visible." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=372&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=372&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=372&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=468&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=468&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761806/original/file-20260923-60-s6lwrz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=468&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A still from the 2004 documentary ‘Wall’ depicts the moment that a section of the West Bank barrier is completed.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5iyA31Tw-7I">Down The Rabbit Hole/YouTube</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Nowhere is this dynamic more evident than the Gaza Strip, which Israel <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/45406228">fenced in during the 1990s</a> and has <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2214163">blockaded since 2007</a>, citing security concerns and the threat of militant attacks.</p>

<p>Thanks to these barriers, the immense suffering of Palestinians in Gaza – <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvgpd1x00exo">more than 70,000</a> of whom have been killed as a result of the Israel-Hamas war since 2023 – has been difficult to document. The Israeli government largely bars international journalists from entering the Gaza Strip independently, while Palestinians in Gaza are generally not allowed to leave the Gaza Strip.</p>

<p>But the Sept. 10, 2026, premiere of Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s film “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt44766123/">NAZA</a>” at the Venice International Film Festival has put the spotlight on the ongoing tragedy in Gaza without relying on footage of gruesome corpses or bombed-out neighborhoods. </p>

<p>The film consists largely of anonymous testimony from 24 members of Israel’s military and intelligence services. They discuss the ways in which <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/11/naza-directors-film-israeli-intelligence-rachel-szor-yuval-abraham-">Israel has used artificial intelligence</a> to target Hamas officials, despite knowing the attacks will also generate large numbers of civilian casualties. The title, “NAZA,” comes from an acronym for the Hebrew phrase “nezek agavi,” or “collateral damage,” and it’s the Israeli military’s threshold system for how many civilian casualties are acceptable in its military strikes on Gaza since <a href="https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/israeli-palestinian-conflict">the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks</a>. Hamas-led militants from Gaza launched those attacks in southern Israel, murdering 1,200 people – mostly civilians – and also taking about 250 hostages.</p>

<p>To me, part of the film’s power lies in its focus on the clinical way of carrying out strikes on Gaza from a distance. But the Israeli military’s approach could only work after systematically isolating the Palestinian people over the course of decades.</p>

<h2>Unseen victims</h2>

<p>In addition to constructing walls and blockading Gaza, Israel has enforced separation of Palestinians <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/14650045.2011.562944">by restricting or denying permits</a> to Palestinians wishing to enter or work in Israel through <a href="https://www.versobooks.com/products/2007-hollow-land">aerial surveillance</a> and <a href="https://www.versobooks.com/products/2007-hollow-land">through the expansion</a> of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.  </p>

<p>Both the visual language and the content of “NAZA” reflect and reveal how knowledge of Palestinian suffering is often mitigated in Israeli culture, politics and daily life. </p>

<p>The film juxtaposes audio of Israeli soldiers’ testimony with shots of the Tel Aviv cityscape at night. In these interviews, the soldiers map out how targets are chosen, how attacks are planned and how much leeway is given for civilian casualties. </p>

<p>The victims themselves are largely unseen, despite their close proximity: Tel Aviv sits a mere 43 miles – or 70 kilometers – up the coast from the Gaza Strip. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Photograph of cityscape with buildings destroyed by bombs and makeshift tents set up." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762121/original/file-20260924-50-tyn04k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Gaza City, shown on Sept. 21, 2026, is just 43 miles from Tel Aviv, yet the two can seem worlds apart.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/view-shows-makeshift-tents-set-up-amidst-damaged-buildings-news-photo/2295916095?adppopup=true">Faiz Qreqa/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The choice to film primarily at night, in darkness, using disembodied voices to tell a story not depicted on camera, further highlights the extent to which these events have been obscured in Israel and around the world. Perhaps that’s why the Israeli government has gone to such great lengths to discredit the film, saying it contains “<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/14/gaza-documentary-makers-naza-israel-citizenship-ntwnfb?">deliberate distortions of reality</a>.” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/world/middleeast/israel-naza-documentary-backlash.html">has threatened to revoke the citizenship of its directors</a>. </p>

<p>In response to the interest and backlash surrounding the film, <a href="https://x.com/yuval_abraham/status/2103061893913162054">the filmmakers announced</a> that “NAZA” will be available to stream for free, for anyone to see, beginning in November 2026.</p>

<h2>Breaking through</h2>

<p>“NAZA” highlights a psychological distance between attacker and attacked that was enabled by AI, computer screens and the physical isolation of the targets. Yet it is far from the first film to call attention to the invisibility of Palestinians.</p>

<p>Elia Suleiman’s 2002 dark comedy “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0274428/">Divine Intervention</a>” repeatedly stages scenes in which Palestinian characters are stuck at or try to get around an Israeli military checkpoint. And Yoav Shamir’s 2003 documentary “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0391857/">Checkpoint</a>” chronicles everyday interactions between Palestinians and Israeli soldiers at checkpoints in the West Bank and Gaza. </p>

<p>Other films center on acts of transgression or protest. Hany Abu-Assad’s 2013 drama “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2852406/">Omar</a>” and Ameen Nayfeh’s 2020 drama “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt12246266/">200 Meters</a>” both feature Palestinian characters who break the law and surreptitiously cross the West Bank border into Israeli territory, exposing themselves to physical and legal danger.</p>

<p>“<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt30953759/">No Other Land</a>” – the 2024 documentary <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-palestinian-israeli-film-just-won-an-oscar-so-why-is-it-so-hard-to-see-249233">that netted Abraham and Szor an Oscar</a>, along with fellow directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal – points the camera on Palestinian protest movements against land expropriations and home demolitions in the West Bank. In the 2011 film “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2125423/">5 Broken Cameras</a>,” Palestinian farmer Emad Burnat captures his West Bank village’s struggle against the construction of a massive wall that chokes off farmland and access to vital resources. Even as his cameras are repeatedly damaged or destroyed, Burnat refuses to stop documenting the resistance.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/40KW6knYMo4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">‘NAZA’ will be available to stream for free starting in November 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Crying while shooting</h2>

<p>“NAZA” also points to another phenomenon: how isolation and separation encourage complicity. The physical distance between Israeli soldiers and the people they target may make it easier to go along with or ignore what is happening.</p>

<p>In this way, “NAZA” grapples with a trope in Israeli films and literature of exploring the guilt of Israeli soldiers. Sometimes derisively referred to by critics as “<a href="https://academic.oup.com/screen/article-abstract/54/1/44/1623426">shooting and crying</a>,” the thematic framework of these films has been criticized for focusing on Israeli moral anguish at the expense of Palestinian experiences and perspectives.</p>

<p>For example, S. Yizhar’s 1949 novel, “Khirbet Khizeh,” which was adapted <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0151202/">into a film</a> in 1978, tells the story from the perspective of Micha, an Israeli soldier fighting in the 1948 war that established the state of Israel. He’s part of a squad that expels Palestinians from their village, and his ensuing guilt provokes a crisis of conscience that haunts him for years to come. </p>

<p>Decades later, the 2008 animated documentary “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1185616/">Waltz With Bashir</a>” follows the film’s director, Ari Folman, as he plumbs his repressed memories of his participation in the <a href="https://www.npr.org/2007/08/28/12744311/timeline-1982-siege-of-beirut">1982 Israeli invasion of Beirut</a> and how he inadvertently helped Lebanese Christian Phalangist militia fighters carry out <a href="https://imeu.org/resources/resources/explainer-the-sabra-shatila-massacre/113">massacres of Palestinians at the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/uWo8U5J0XeY?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">‘Waltz With Bashir’ centered on the fragmented memories, trauma and guilt of an Israeli soldier who had helped facilitate the Sabra and Shatila massacre in Beirut, Lebanon, in 1982.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The “shooting and crying” genre was largely accepted in mainstream Israeli culture, with “Khirbet Khizeh” <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/1/article/963600/summary">taught in Israeli schools</a> for decades. But the Israeli government’s hostile reaction to “NAZA” perhaps signals not only the growing intolerance of dissent in Israel, but also a <a href="https://contendingmodernities.nd.edu/global-currents/shooting-and-singing/">fading cultural and political concern</a> with the morality of Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory.</p>

<h2>Whose voices get heard</h2>

<p>The centering of Israeli perspectives in these earlier works – as well as in “NAZA” – also shows how violence against Palestinians can be given greater credence when it’s described by Israelis themselves. </p>

<p>Recent Palestinian narratives about Gaza, such as “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt32606918/">From Ground Zero</a>” and “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt43743832/">Thirteen in Gaza</a>,” have garnered <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2025/sep/09/from-ground-zero-stories-from-gaza-review-scenes-of-ordinary-life-in-extremis">some attention and praise</a> in <a href="https://deadline.com/2026/09/thirteen-gaza-trailer-father-daughter-palestinian-netpac-1237109243/">the film world</a>, but nowhere near the same amount as “NAZA” has in the weeks since its premiere.</p>

<p>Even “No Other Land,” which is centered on a Palestinian village, features an Israeli journalist and filmmaker, Abraham, documenting the protests and confronting Israeli soldiers, and may not have received the same acclaim if it had been made entirely by Palestinians. </p>

<p>Yet, despite these many barriers, Palestinians have never stopped finding ways to make themselves heard. In addition to films like “Omar” and “200 Meters,” videos and images <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/14781158.2024.2415908">shared directly to social media</a> have allowed Palestinians to connect directly with audiences and shape global awareness of their plight, especially since the current war in Gaza began. </p>

<p>They have been able to bypass the physical barriers that have long restricted their movement – and the cultural barriers that have often kept their experiences out of sight.</p>

body: 'NAZA' filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor conducted interviews with anonymous members of Israeli military and intelligence services from the rooftops of Tel Aviv, Israel

Gil Cohen-Magen/AFP via Getty Images There’s a powerful scene in Moroccan-French-Israeli filmmaker Simone Bitton’s 2004 documentary “ Wall ,” which tells the story of the construction of the West Bank barrier , a 448-mile – or 721-kilometer – network of walls and fences dividing large parts of the West Bank from Israel
A concrete slab is slowly lowered into place in order to complete a section of the wall
Inch by inch, the vibrant, hilly Palestinian community on the other side gets smaller and smaller
And then – just like that – a world that’s a stone’s throw away is gone

As someone who studies the restrictions placed on Palestinians, I often think about this scene as a microcosm of Israel’s decades-long use of walls, checkpoints and surveillance technologies to seal off Palestinians from the rest of society
A still from the 2004 documentary ‘Wall’ depicts the moment that a section of the West Bank barrier is completed

Down The Rabbit Hole/YouTube Nowhere is this dynamic more evident than the Gaza Strip, which Israel fenced in during the 1990s and has blockaded since 2007 , citing security concerns and the threat of militant attacks
Thanks to these barriers, the immense suffering of Palestinians in Gaza – more than 70,000 of whom have been killed as a result of the Israel-Hamas war since 2023 – has been difficult to document
The Israeli government largely bars international journalists from entering the Gaza Strip independently, while Palestinians in Gaza are generally not allowed to leave the Gaza Strip

But the Sept. 10, 2026, premiere of Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s film “ NAZA ” at the Venice International Film Festival has put the spotlight on the ongoing tragedy in Gaza without relying on footage of gruesome corpses or bombed-out neighborhoods
The film consists largely of anonymous testimony from 24 members of Israel’s military and intelligence services
They discuss the ways in which Israel has used artificial intelligence to target Hamas officials, despite knowing the attacks will also generate large numbers of civilian casualties

The title, “NAZA,” comes from an acronym for the Hebrew phrase “nezek agavi,” or “collateral damage,” and it’s the Israeli military’s threshold system for how many civilian casualties are acceptable in its military strikes on Gaza since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks
Hamas-led militants from Gaza launched those attacks in southern Israel, murdering 1,200 people – mostly civilians – and also taking about 250 hostages
To me, part of the film’s power lies in its focus on the clinical way of carrying out strikes on Gaza from a distance
But the Israeli military’s approach could only work after systematically isolating the Palestinian people over the course of decades

Unseen victims In addition to constructing walls and blockading Gaza, Israel has enforced separation of Palestinians by restricting or denying permits to Palestinians wishing to enter or work in Israel through aerial surveillance and through the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank
Both the visual language and the content of “NAZA” reflect and reveal how knowledge of Palestinian suffering is often mitigated in Israeli culture, politics and daily life
The film juxtaposes audio of Israeli soldiers’ testimony with shots of the Tel Aviv cityscape at night
In these interviews, the soldiers map out how targets are chosen, how attacks are planned and how much leeway is given for civilian casualties
The victims themselves are largely unseen, despite their close proximity: Tel Aviv sits a mere 43 miles – or 70 kilometers – up the coast from the Gaza Strip
Gaza City, shown on Sept. 21, 2026, is just 43 miles from Tel Aviv, yet the two can seem worlds apart

Faiz Qreqa/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images The choice to film primarily at night, in darkness, using disembodied voices to tell a story not depicted on camera, further highlights the extent to which these events have been obscured in Israel and around the world

Perhaps that’s why the Israeli government has gone to such great lengths to discredit the film, saying it contains “ deliberate distortions of reality .” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened to revoke the citizenship of its directors
In response to the interest and backlash surrounding the film, the filmmakers announced that “NAZA” will be available to stream for free, for anyone to see, beginning in November 2026
Breaking through “NAZA” highlights a psychological distance between attacker and attacked that was enabled by AI, computer screens and the physical isolation of the targets
Yet it is far from the first film to call attention to the invisibility of Palestinians
Elia Suleiman’s 2002 dark comedy “ Divine Intervention ” repeatedly stages scenes in which Palestinian characters are stuck at or try to get around an Israeli military checkpoint
And Yoav Shamir’s 2003 documentary “ Checkpoint ” chronicles everyday interactions between Palestinians and Israeli soldiers at checkpoints in the West Bank and Gaza
Other films center on acts of transgression or protest

Hany Abu-Assad’s 2013 drama “ Omar ” and Ameen Nayfeh’s 2020 drama “ 200 Meters ” both feature Palestinian characters who break the law and surreptitiously cross the West Bank border into Israeli territory, exposing themselves to physical and legal danger. “ No Other Land ” – the 2024 documentary that netted Abraham and Szor an Oscar , along with fellow directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal – points the camera on Palestinian protest movements against land expropriations and home demolitions in the West Bank

In the 2011 film “ 5 Broken Cameras ,” Palestinian farmer Emad Burnat captures his West Bank village’s struggle against the construction of a massive wall that chokes off farmland and access to vital resources
Even as his cameras are repeatedly damaged or destroyed, Burnat refuses to stop documenting the resistance. ‘NAZA’ will be available to stream for free starting in November 2026
Crying while shooting “NAZA” also points to another phenomenon: how isolation and separation encourage complicity
The physical distance between Israeli soldiers and the people they target may make it easier to go along with or ignore what is happening
In this way, “NAZA” grapples with a trope in Israeli films and literature of exploring the guilt of Israeli soldiers

Sometimes derisively referred to by critics as “ shooting and crying ,” the thematic framework of these films has been criticized for focusing on Israeli moral anguish at the expense of Palestinian experiences and perspectives

Yizhar’s 1949 novel, “Khirbet Khizeh,” which was adapted into a film in 1978, tells the story from the perspective of Micha, an Israeli soldier fighting in the 1948 war that established the state of Israel
He’s part of a squad that expels Palestinians from their village, and his ensuing guilt provokes a crisis of conscience that haunts him for years to come

<title>Trump has gotten rid of many of the checks and balances that could stop him from demolishing the Kennedy Center</title>

Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on Sept. 18, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Trump%20Kennedy%20Center/d0e3631e03724912b6556e5ffb0b4d5c/photo">AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Who gets to decide the future of the <a href="https://www.kennedy-center.org/memorial/">living memorial to former President John F. Kennedy</a>, and who holds those decision-makers to account?</p>

<p>This debate is becoming ever more fraught. A <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/17/us/politics/trump-kennedy-center-photos.html">photo taken on Sept. 16, 2026</a>, showed President Donald J. Trump in Air Force One reviewing a poster with the words “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH …” that many interpreted to mean “demolished.”</p>

<p>The image spread quickly. Like the protests that brought <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/protesters-plan-form-human-chain-kennedy-center-amid/story?id=136558872">throngs of arts lovers to the center a few days later</a>, it amplified the drama around the fate of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C. For more than a half-century, the multivenue complex has featured world-class symphonies, operas, dance and theater performances, along with education programs. </p>

<p>Whether it would be <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/17/arts/music/kennedy-center-closure-emergency-hearing.html">open or closed</a> to the public, active or dormant, repaired or dismantled, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/13/arts/design/trump-kennedy-center-bankruptcy-closure.html">solvent or bankrupt</a> and if it can <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/09/15/trump-kennedy-center-judge/a43ae64a-b123-11f1-92c2-5c918f4a6127_story.html">include Trump’s name in its branding</a> have been the subjects of widespread dispute and speculation since Trump returned to office.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://www.american.edu/cas/faculty/eataylor.cfm">professor and scholar of arts management</a>, I can explain why the official answers to who gets to decide and who is supposed to hold those deciders accountable are reasonably clear.</p>

<h2>Oversight hierarchy collapsed</h2>

<p>Congress <a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?hl=false&amp;edition=2023&amp;req=granuleid%3AUSC-2018-title20-chapter3-subchapter5&amp;num=0">created the Kennedy Center and determines its governance</a>. It’s up to lawmakers, through their power of the purse, to decide on funding for construction, repairs and a portion of its operational budget.</p>

<p>The oversight of facilities and programs falls to a board of trustees that’s authorized by Congress to advance the mission and secure the majority of the center’s earned and contributed revenue. And those operations are, in turn, subject to review by the Internal Revenue Service, which determines the center’s nonprofit status, and federal courts, which determine its compliance with the law.</p>

<p>So how did that hierarchy of oversight essentially collapse into <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/siladityaray/2026/09/16/democrat-says-trump-threw-tantrum-during-kennedy-center-board-meeting-after-court-ruling/">a shouting match between Trump and Rep. Joyce Beatty</a>, an Ohio Democrat, and result in two ongoing lawsuits in U.S. District Court?</p>

<p>Beatty <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/district-of-columbia/dcdce/1:2025cv04480/287972/50/">filed one of the suits</a> and <a href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/72528661/dc-preservation-league-v-board-of-trustees-of-the-john-f-kennedy-center/">a consortium of architects and preservationists</a> filed the other. <a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/judge-kennedy-center-case-orders-trump-administration-explain-closure-plans-2026-09-16/">The same judge</a>, Christopher R. Cooper, is presiding over both cases.</p>



<h2>Presidential control</h2>

<p>The main cause of what I would call a governance failure is that most of those official oversight authorities now serve at the pleasure of the president.</p>

<p>In 2025, the Republican-controlled Congress <a href="https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/kennedy-center-faces-257-million-renovation-what-one-big-beautiful-bill-really-covers-1775497">approved US$257 million</a> for “necessary expenses for capital repair, restoration, maintenance backlog, and security structures” at the Kennedy Center. But most GOP legislators have remained silent about its oversight, including multiple attempts to affix Trump’s name to the building – which <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/09/15/judge-blocks-kennedy-center-trump-name-inscription-sign/91775374007/">Judge Cooper keeps insisting</a> is something only Congress can allow. </p>

<p>Trump has chaired its board of trustees and appointed the vast majority of its members since <a href="https://theconversation.com/trump-has-purged-the-kennedy-centers-board-which-in-turn-made-him-its-chair-why-does-that-matter-249934">an unprecedented restructuring to the previously bipartisan board</a> in February 2025.</p>

<p>In his <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/district-of-columbia/dcdce/1:2025cv04480/287972/50/">May 2026 ruling</a>, Judge Cooper found the board of trustees to be “derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center.” More recently, the DC Preservation League has suggested <a href="https://dcpreservation.org/2026/09/17/plaintiffs-call-for-independent-protection-of-the-kennedy-center/">removal of the trustees and appointment of a receiver</a> if current leadership “is unwilling or unable to exercise its fiduciary duty.”</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762147/original/file-20260924-50-xgvjta.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large building faces a river." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762147/original/file-20260924-50-xgvjta.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762147/original/file-20260924-50-xgvjta.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762147/original/file-20260924-50-xgvjta.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762147/original/file-20260924-50-xgvjta.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762147/original/file-20260924-50-xgvjta.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762147/original/file-20260924-50-xgvjta.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762147/original/file-20260924-50-xgvjta.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<h2>Agencies aren’t responding</h2>

<p>With both Congress and the trustees aligned with Trump, there are several federal agencies that could be stepping in to critique the board or its decisions: the Internal Revenue Service, the Justice Department, the Office of Management and Budget and others.</p>

<p>But they are all cooperating with the White House in a dramatic consolidation of power by the executive branch that <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/06/29/nx-s1-5816232/supreme-court-ftc-independent-agencies-humphreys-executor">now reaches into traditionally independent federal agencies</a>.</p>

<p>That leaves the federal courts, where Beatty is among the few with standing to sue. She is an <a href="https://www.wsj.com/opinion/stolen-glory-at-the-kennedy-center-121a327f">ex officio member of the board</a>, meaning that she serves by virtue of her role in Congress. She also is willing to stand up and challenge the Trump administration’s attempt to direct – and perhaps even demolish – the Kennedy Center.</p>

<p>Even as these and other construction-related lawsuits are pending, the Trump administration has proven its willingness and ability to build, renovate or destroy federal landmarks without clear authority to do so.</p>

<p>Trump had the White House <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/new-images-show-entire-white-house-east-wing/story?id=126800684">East Wing demolished</a> in October 2025 without getting Congress to sign off or sharing those plans in advance. And he has <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-shows-off-multimillion-dollar-white-house-helipad/story?id=135782264">built a new helipad</a> on White House grounds, to name two examples.</p>

<p>Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts has called Trump’s attempt to build a ballroom where the East Wing used to stand without congressional authorization “<a href="https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/6062155-roberts-white-house-ballroom-dissent/">likely unlawful</a>.” And yet, construction continues.</p>

Kennedy looks out over an expanse of red carpet." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762143/original/file-20260924-50-yu6se1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762143/original/file-20260924-50-yu6se1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762143/original/file-20260924-50-yu6se1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762143/original/file-20260924-50-yu6se1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762143/original/file-20260924-50-yu6se1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762143/original/file-20260924-50-yu6se1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762143/original/file-20260924-50-yu6se1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Who decides?</h2>

<p>The buildings on the Kennedy Center campus are only part of what’s at stake.</p>

<p>The Kennedy Center was established as a “living memorial” to former President John F. Kennedy. The “memorial” part is largely associated with the physical campus and its many engravings and artworks honoring Kennedy.</p>

<p>But the “living” component manifests in its live performances, original productions, educational programming, artistic leadership and what audiences, educators and students experience both within and beyond the campus walls.</p>

<p>There were early indicators that both programs and public engagement were faltering under the board’s new leadership. Revenue from performances <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/entertainment/2025/12/07/trump-kennedy-center">began a steep decline</a> after Trump’s takeover in February 2025, well before he announced his intention to <a href="https://theconversation.com/trump-wants-to-shutter-the-kennedy-center-for-2-years-an-arts-management-professor-explains-what-that-portends-274906">close the center for major repairs</a>. It wasn’t just audiences turning away – many artists also <a href="https://www.newsweek.com/entertainment/full-list-acts-pulled-out-trump-changed-kennedy-center-name-11451229">canceled their engagements</a> or stopped making customary bookings.</p>

<p>Prior to that takeover, The Washington Post has reported, the center’s finances had <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/style/2026/08/25/kennedy-center-revenue-plunged-after-trumps-name-went-building/">become increasingly strong</a> as it <a href="https://www.kennedy-center.org/globalassets/our-story/mission/kennedy-center-fy24-budget-justification-to-congress.pdf">recovered from the disruptions</a> that all arts venues suffered during the COVID-19 pandemic. </p>

<p>So, who gets to decide the future of this living memorial to a <a href="https://www.aarp.org/events-history/why-we-love-john-f-kennedy">revered slain president</a>? In the short term, it’s the center’s board, chaired by Trump. And who holds those decision-makers to account? Ongoing federal court cases have constrained or delayed some of those choices. But most other official checks and balances are currently neutral or skewed in the president’s favor. </p>

<p>Public attention through independent journalism and <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/protesters-plan-form-human-chain-kennedy-center-amid/story?id=136558872">citizen activism</a> can increase friction and shape the political calculus surrounding the Kennedy Center. But any long-term solution will depend on the physical condition of its campus, its adherence to its original mission as a living memorial and the reliable, responsible and accountable governance of its leaders.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292436/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana Who gets to decide the future of the living memorial to former President John F
Kennedy , and who holds those decision-makers to account? This debate is becoming ever more fraught
A photo taken on Sept. 16, 2026 , showed President Donald J
Trump in Air Force One reviewing a poster with the words “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH …” that many interpreted to mean “demolished.” The image spread quickly
Like the protests that brought throngs of arts lovers to the center a few days later , it amplified the drama around the fate of the John F
Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C
For more than a half-century, the multivenue complex has featured world-class symphonies, operas, dance and theater performances, along with education programs

Whether it would be open or closed to the public, active or dormant, repaired or dismantled, solvent or bankrupt and if it can include Trump’s name in its branding have been the subjects of widespread dispute and speculation since Trump returned to office
As a professor and scholar of arts management , I can explain why the official answers to who gets to decide and who is supposed to hold those deciders accountable are reasonably clear
President Trump is seen aboard Air Force One on Sept. 16, 2026, reading a sign that suggested he might have the Kennedy Center demolished
Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Oversight hierarchy collapsed Congress created the Kennedy Center and determines its governance
It’s up to lawmakers, through their power of the purse, to decide on funding for construction, repairs and a portion of its operational budget
The oversight of facilities and programs falls to a board of trustees that’s authorized by Congress to advance the mission and secure the majority of the center’s earned and contributed revenue
And those operations are, in turn, subject to review by the Internal Revenue Service, which determines the center’s nonprofit status, and federal courts, which determine its compliance with the law
So how did that hierarchy of oversight essentially collapse into a shouting match between Trump and Rep
Joyce Beatty , an Ohio Democrat, and result in two ongoing lawsuits in U.S
District Court? Beatty filed one of the suits and a consortium of architects and preservationists filed the other
Presidential control The main cause of what I would call a governance failure is that most of those official oversight authorities now serve at the pleasure of the president
In 2025, the Republican-controlled Congress approved US$257 million for “necessary expenses for capital repair, restoration, maintenance backlog, and security structures” at the Kennedy Center

But most GOP legislators have remained silent about its oversight, including multiple attempts to affix Trump’s name to the building – which Judge Cooper keeps insisting is something only Congress can allow
Trump has chaired its board of trustees and appointed the vast majority of its members since an unprecedented restructuring to the previously bipartisan board in February 2025

In his May 2026 ruling , Judge Cooper found the board of trustees to be “derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center.” More recently, the DC Preservation League has suggested removal of the trustees and appointment of a receiver if current leadership “is unwilling or unable to exercise its fiduciary duty.” The John F
Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts is seen from the air on Aug. 30, 2026

AP Photo/Alex Brandon Agencies aren’t responding With both Congress and the trustees aligned with Trump, there are several federal agencies that could be stepping in to critique the board or its decisions: the Internal Revenue Service, the Justice Department, the Office of Management and Budget and others
But they are all cooperating with the White House in a dramatic consolidation of power by the executive branch that now reaches into traditionally independent federal agencies
That leaves the federal courts, where Beatty is among the few with standing to sue
She is an ex officio member of the board , meaning that she serves by virtue of her role in Congress
She also is willing to stand up and challenge the Trump administration’s attempt to direct – and perhaps even demolish – the Kennedy Center

Even as these and other construction-related lawsuits are pending, the Trump administration has proven its willingness and ability to build, renovate or destroy federal landmarks without clear authority to do so
Trump had the White House East Wing demolished in October 2025 without getting Congress to sign off or sharing those plans in advance
And he has built a new helipad on White House grounds, to name two examples

Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts has called Trump’s attempt to build a ballroom where the East Wing used to stand without congressional authorization “ likely unlawful .” And yet, construction continues
It was hard for arts patrons to miss this large bust of John F
Kennedy looking out over the foyer outside the Kennedy Center’s Opera House
Nikki Kahn/The Washington Post via Getty Images Who decides? The buildings on the Kennedy Center campus are only part of what’s at stake
The Kennedy Center was established as a “living memorial” to former President John F
The “memorial” part is largely associated with the physical campus and its many engravings and artworks honoring Kennedy

But the “living” component manifests in its live performances, original productions, educational programming, artistic leadership and what audiences, educators and students experience both within and beyond the campus walls

<title>Trump frames unregulated AI as a way to keep ahead of China – but in fact, it harms US national security</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762150/original/file-20260924-50-b3v7d2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7548%2C5032&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Are Presidents Trump and Xi walking down a dangerous path on AI?</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-donald-trump-walks-with-chinas-president-xi-news-photo/2296275067?adppopup=true">Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Amid the chorus of voices calling for <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/12/anthropic-ceo-dario-amodei-seeks-immediate-slowdown-artificial-intelligence-01073519">a slowdown in AI advancement</a> and <a href="https://abcnews.com/US/23-states-urge-congress-regulate-ai-warn-risks/story?id=136711204">more government regulation</a> and oversight of the technology, one prominent contrarian voice stands out: that of Donald J. Trump.</p>

<p>The U.S president has repeatedly argued that the introduction of robust regulations to slow down progress on AI <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6089123-trump-resists-ai-regulation-warnings/">threatens U.S. national interests</a> by enabling China to seize the advantage.</p>

<p>“Whoever wins AI, WINS!” Trump <a href="http://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117269745153543631">posted on social media</a> on Sept. 21, 2026, and singled out China as the primary threat to America “winning” AI. He followed up with a speech at the United Nations in which he <a href="https://thehill.com/newsletters/6104340-report/6104340-trump-tells-un-that-ai-needs-a-rebrand/amp/">outlined his administration’s total rejection</a> of “any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” artificial intelligence.</p>

<p>Certainly, China seizing the global lead on AI would represent an alarming setback to American strategic and economic interests. As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=dMo5aFUAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">scholar whose research examines the intersection</a> of international relations and technology, I contend that China’s swift advances in AI constitute one of the leading reasons why regulation of the U.S. AI industry is necessary. Paradoxical as it may sound, slowing down AI advancement in the U.S. would also decelerate China’s advances. </p>

<p>Even more important, recent <a href="https://theconversation.com/government-hacks-rogue-agents-and-no-transparency-can-we-ever-fully-trust-ai-292536">revelations about AI “going rogue,”</a> coupled with the astonishing <a href="https://fortune.com/2026/02/24/anthropic-china-deepseek-theft-claude-distillation-copyright-national-security/">growth in power and capability of new AI models</a>, strongly suggest that an unregulated sector represents a greater security threat for the United States than the threat of a surge in capabilities by China.  </p>

<h2>Unregulated AI and security threats</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/12/technology/anthropic-dario-amodei-ai-slowdown.html">Leading industry</a> and <a href="https://www.un.org/unispal/document/sg-address-unga-81-22sep26/">political figures</a> around the globe have sounded the alarm about the security threats presented by unchecked AI growth. About 8 in 10 <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/24/politics/cnn-poll-ai-data-centers-vis">Americans share these concerns</a>, according to recent polling, as a large majority of Democrats, Independents and Republicans support increasing AI regulations.</p>

<p>These threats include heightened U.S. vulnerability to attacks from foreign nations and <a href="https://unicri.org/News/Algorithms-Terrorism-UNICRI-UNOCCT">terrorist groups who can exploit AI advances</a> to build <a href="https://hms.harvard.edu/news/risks-artificial-intelligence-weapons-design">more lethal weapons systems</a> – both conventional arms and weapons of mass destruction. Advances in the sector also increase the chance of nefarious actors launching devastating cyberattacks, with <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/five-eyes-intelligence-alliance-warns-that-new-ai-models-pose-urgent-cyber-risk-2026-06-22/?utm_source=chatgpt.com">AI becoming increasingly adept</a> at identifying and exploiting cybersecurity vulnerabilities.</p>

<p>These concerns are known within the industry. On Sept. 10, 2026, Anthropic <a href="http://bbc.com/news/articles/cx2zrrpkx20o?accountMarketingPreferences=off">issued a report</a> revealing a series of incidents in which foreign actors – some based in China, Russia and Iran – used Claude in cyber, influence, surveillance and fraud operations and to support weapons development. Google similarly detected recent attempts by actors linked to China, Russia, North Korea and Iran to <a href="https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/from-prompting-to-autonomy-the-evolution-of-adversarial-ai">use its Gemini AI model</a> to carry out hacking, disinformation, espionage and criminal operations.</p>

<p>Anthropic’s <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026">report revealed</a> “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development.” </p>

<p>Unregulated AI poses not just a severe security challenge but a <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-would-ai-actually-kill-all-humans-here-are-the-top-5-scenarios-292220">potentially existential threat</a>. An AI-induced nuclear missile launch, the release of super pathogens that cause pandemics and attacks on critical life-sustaining infrastructure have all been raised as potential concerns. Aside from these more extreme scenarios, unchecked AI poses a threat to the digital infrastructure that undergirds the U.S. and world economies.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762296/original/file-20260925-50-me9pn7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Four men on a red carpet speak to dozens of people holding cameras and microphones." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762296/original/file-20260925-50-me9pn7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762296/original/file-20260925-50-me9pn7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762296/original/file-20260925-50-me9pn7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762296/original/file-20260925-50-me9pn7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762296/original/file-20260925-50-me9pn7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762296/original/file-20260925-50-me9pn7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762296/original/file-20260925-50-me9pn7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<h2>Slowing the speedboat</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cw980n0nd0qjo">Trump may dismiss these worst-case scenarios</a> as a “hoax,” but the national security threats are real. Trump’s argument is that the best way to protect the U.S. is to make sure American companies stay ahead of China on AI. Indeed, China’s AI models are not far behind, and China possesses an advantage in a factor vital to AI systems – <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/23/us/politics/ai-us-china-trump-xi-economy.html">electric power generation</a>, which AI consumes in large and growing quantities. </p>

<p>Still, the consensus of tech experts is that the U.S. remains the world’s top AI power due to American firms’ lead in <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/23/us/politics/ai-us-china-trump-xi-economy.html">advanced models and computer chips</a> and the scale of America’s computing power – through chips, processors and servers – as well as <a href="https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report">the level of capital investment</a>.  </p>

<p>However, the rapid advance of AI capabilities by American firms has helped China to accelerate its own AI industry.</p>

<p>China <a href="https://fortune.com/2026/02/24/anthropic-china-deepseek-theft-claude-distillation-copyright-national-security/">uses a process known as distillation</a> to exploit cutting-edge U.S. AI models to train China’s own models. The process enables China to develop models nearly as powerful but much more efficient, using far fewer resources.</p>

<p>Beijing’s reliance on distillation, according to <a href="https://carnegieendowment.org/people/matt-sheehan">Matt Sheehan</a>, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, is a result of its own limited computing power, estimated at just one-tenth that of the United States. As a result of its distillation strategy, the pace of <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/15/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-matt-sheehan.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share">China’s AI progress is tightly linked to U.S. progress</a>. Using Sheenan’s analogy, the relationship is much like a speedboat pulling a water skier: If the U.S. eases on the AI throttle, China will be forced to slow down as well.</p>

<p>Therefore, racing ahead unchecked at breakneck speed – the approach advocated by Trump – would not guarantee that the U.S. widens its AI lead. Chinese firms will continue to exploit U.S. AI progress to <a href="https://thediplomat.com/2026/08/chinas-military-is-now-using-ai-to-plan-strike-operations/">strengthen their offensive capabilities</a>.</p>

<h2>Global governance and regulation</h2>

<p>As such, rather than jeopardizing American national security, U.S. regulations that slow AI advancement could strengthen security by slowing down the Chinese government’s own access to cutting-edge AI.</p>

<p>The “China threat” argument against greater U.S. regulation on AI is also predicated on the notion that Beijing does not possess its own concerns about the dangers of unchecked growth in AI power, and this isn’t the case. </p>

<p>Chinese leaders harbor serious security and domestic affairs–related <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/world/asia/china-ai-security-risks-anthropic.html">concerns about uncontrolled AI growth</a>. Indeed, if there is one AI area where China leads the U.S., it is in regulations on AI. Consider, for example, that as far back as 2021, Beijing imposed its <a href="https://carnegieendowment.org/research/2024/02/tracing-the-roots-of-chinas-ai-regulations?utm_source=chatgpt.com">first major set of AI regulations</a>.</p>

<p>And while top figures in the Trump administration were urging less regulation, Chinese officials were calling for the opposite. In recent months, Chinese officials have repeatedly called for greater <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/09/25/trump-rejects-demands-ai-rules-while-xi-calls-human-control/">domestic and international oversight of AI</a>. China’s leader, Xi Jinping, has been enthusiastic about AI advances, but his speech at the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai urgently <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/ddb316b4-c6ae-4b9b-9d4a-63d63201d4fc?utm_source=chatgpt.com&amp;syn-25a6b1a6=1">expressed the need for strong AI regulations and oversight</a>.</p>

<p>Speaking at the U.N. Security Council’s meeting on AI and International Security on Sept. 23, 2026, Fu Cong, China’s permanent representative to the United Nations, <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/us-chinese-visions-for-ai-regulation-differ-sharply-at-un-meeting-01090906">made the case for</a> “a consensus-based global governance framework” for AI to “build institutional guardrails that preserve international peace and security.”</p>

<p>Beijing appears to be framing unregulated AI advancement not as a race but as a common threat. Should Trump be convinced by such a narrative, then there may be grounds for optimism that Washington and Beijing in the near future will be able to reach agreement on AI governance and regulation – a development that would better ensure a safer future for both nations.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292642/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Gen Z communicates differently in the workplace, but older colleagues can still decode them</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762017/original/file-20260924-72-xnnd8i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5184%2C3456&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Young workers often share values with older colleagues, but the environment where they learned about workplace behavior is different.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/a-man-sitting-in-front-of-a-laptop-computer-7nQGQ0ve5A0">Sebastian Herrmann on Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>For all the talk about <a href="https://theconversation.com/young-professionals-are-struggling-to-socially-adapt-in-the-workplace-educators-can-help-237845">generational differences</a> at work, some of the biggest differences show up in surprisingly ordinary moments.</p>

<p>Take being late for work. A <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2019/01/17/where-millennials-end-and-generation-z-begins/">Gen Z</a> employee in her 20s I spoke with works at a small, locally owned café and restaurant run by an older Gen X owner. When she realized she was going to be late one day, she texted him. He was frustrated. To him, being late was serious enough to warrant a phone call, and a text felt too casual and impersonal. </p>

<p>She saw the exact same interaction very differently. </p>

<p>“He’s super busy, so I felt a call was going to take up too much time,” she told me. “So I texted. I thought it was more considerate.” </p>

<p>Both thought they understood what respectful workplace communication looked like. They just had completely different definitions of it.</p>

<p><a href="https://jeffleblancdba.com/">I study workplace culture</a> and communication, and I see this type of misunderstanding as increasingly common in multigenerational workplaces. And this is becoming more pronounced as Gen Z moves further into the workforce. The <a href="https://www.fastcompany.com/91369085/ready-or-not-gen-z-is-managing-you-gen-z-work-management">oldest members of Gen Z</a> are now approaching 30, while the youngest are in college and high school.</p>

<p>What’s distinctive about the older members of Gen Z is that many went through college, internships or their first jobs <a href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0249792&amp;utm">during the COVID-19 pandemic</a>, when much of our communication moved online and masks often covered half our faces. And there’s a new twist now, as artificial intelligence changes how we communicate all over again. </p>

<p>The result isn’t necessarily that Gen Z employees communicate better or worse with their bosses and colleagues than previous generations did. I argue that they have simply learned to do so in a very different environment.</p>

<h2>When a text means something more</h2>

<p>The café example is an easy one to dismiss as younger workers <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/08934215.2025.2542562">preferring texting</a> and feeling that phone calls are for important occasions only. </p>

<p>But that misses what I think is the more interesting point: The employee wasn’t trying to avoid her boss. She thought she was respecting his time. </p>

<p>For her boss, by contrast, the phone call itself carried meaning. It communicated that she understood the seriousness of being late. </p>

<p>Neither one had explained that expectation to the other.</p>

<p>Managers shouldn’t assume employees attach the same meaning they do to a particular form of communication. If being late requires a phone call, they need to say so. A two-minute conversation about expectations can prevent both people from walking away from an interaction believing the other was disrespectful.</p>

<p>Another common stumble concerns openness, which might feel like oversharing.</p>

<p>One Gen Z worker I spoke with had recently started a job at a large New England company in a blue-collar industry. He was struggling with severe anxiety and decided to tell his <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2008/06/25/baby-boomers-the-gloomiest-generation/">baby boomer</a> manager. The manager was sympathetic, but also uneasy. </p>

<p>“It made me feel uncomfortable, if I’m being honest,” the manager told me. “I didn’t want to downplay his anxiety, but I’m not sure I needed to know.”</p>

<p>That distinction matters. His reaction wasn’t that anxiety wasn’t real or that his employee should simply get over it. But he questioned how much of it belonged in their professional relationship. </p>

<p>Many older workers learned that professionalism is about setting clear boundaries between personal and professional life. Members of Gen Z are coming of age during a period when conversations about <a href="https://hbr.org/2019/10/research-people-want-their-employers-to-talk-about-mental-health">mental health</a> and personal well-being are considerably more public. What feels like honesty to one person can feel like oversharing to their boss. </p>

<p>This doesn’t mean that managers have to become therapists, and employees don’t have to disclose everything happening in their lives. But both may need to recognize that their comfort level around disclosure isn’t universal.</p>

<h2>Learning to read a room when the room disappeared</h2>

<p>Some workplace communication is never spoken at all. Think about how people traditionally learned to read a room. They watched faces around a conference table. They noticed a change in a manager’s tone. Someone caught them after a meeting and quietly explained what had just happened. </p>

<p>Now think about someone who was 18 or 19 in 2020.</p>

<p>At exactly the age when many young people would have been developing these skills in college, internships and early jobs, the room disappeared. Classes went online. Internships became remote. When people returned in person, masks sometimes made facial communication more difficult. </p>

<p>That doesn’t mean members of Gen Z can’t read facial expressions, but we should be careful about assuming everyone had the same opportunities to learn the unwritten signals of professional life. If feedback matters, I believe managers should say it. A disappointed expression on a Zoom call is a poor substitute for a conversation.</p>

<h2>I thought that was understood</h2>

<p>Imagine a manager telling a young employee: “I need this by Friday.” The employee sends it back at 4:30 p.m. that Friday afternoon. The manager is annoyed because they intended to review it that morning, make changes and send it along to someone else. </p>

<p>The employee is equally confused. The deadline was Friday, and they met it.</p>

<p>This deadline mismatch gets at something I have repeatedly encountered in my research with Gen Z workers. <a href="https://al-kindipublisher.com/index.php/jbms/article/view/12577">In a survey</a> I conducted of 250 Gen Z professionals across industries, clear structural expectations emerged alongside fairness and empathetic engagement as recurring themes.</p>

<p>If an <a href="https://www.fastcompany.com/91281732/gen-z-isnt-quiet-quitting-theyre-rejecting-outdated-leadership">employee wants clarity</a>, it shouldn’t automatically be confused with hand-holding. An employee can want autonomy and still want to know exactly what success looks like. “Friday” and “Friday by 10 a.m. because I need three hours to review this” communicate very different expectations.</p>

<p>Artificial intelligence may make this issue even more important. We can now produce polished emails, summarize meetings and generate information faster than ever. But more communication does not guarantee more understanding.</p>

<p>I believe that may be the larger lesson for every generation working together. We tend to mistake the workplace norms we learned for common sense. They aren’t. They were taught to us by the workplaces, technologies and moments in history in which we began our careers.</p>

<p>Gen Z is learning theirs in a very different world.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292108/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>What civil rights enforcement cuts mean for students with disabilities – fewer staff, closed offices, longer waits</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754969/original/file-20260819-50-n81njt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=1489%2C995%2C5735%2C3823&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The Department of Education has undergone various changes, including closing regional offices of its Office for Civil Rights, since 2025.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/lettering-marks-the-entrance-of-the-u-s-department-of-news-photo/2196638450?adppopup=true">J. David Ake/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Felicita Piñón weighed just 1 pound at birth. She was later diagnosed with cerebral palsy that requires her to use a power wheelchair, and she also has learning and emotional challenges. Yet despite these obstacles, Felicita, now an eighth grade student, is just like any other happy, active teenager who hasn’t let her disability limit her. She also did something remarkable that’s not typical of most teens – in 2025, she testified against a school voucher bill at the Texas Capitol. </p>

<p>But in 2024, when Felicita wanted to join a cheerleading team at her Crowley, Texas, middle school, her mother, Liz Piñón, said the school was not willing to make accommodations for her, as she felt <a href="https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/individuals-disabilities">federal disabilities laws</a> required. She believed the school was discriminating against her daughter on the basis of her disability, as well as her race. She also noted that she knew of other nearby schools that had girls in wheelchairs who participated on cheerleading teams. </p>

<p>As a result, Piñón – <a href="https://www.ed.gov/media/document/ocr-report-president-and-secretary-of-education-2024-109012.pdf">like thousands of others that year</a> – filed a complaint with the federal Education Department’s <a href="https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-offices/ocr">Office for Civil Rights</a>. </p>

<p>For decades, the Office for Civil Rights, or OCR, served as a critical safety net when local schools <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/06/16/nx-s1-5717030/special-ed-civil-rights-education-department">failed to meet federal</a> disability standards. Now, <a href="https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/special-ed-and-civil-rights-what-we-know-about-the-ed-dept-s-latest-moves/2026/06">sweeping budget and workforce cuts</a> have restructured the office, leading to the <a href="https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-108320">dismissal of thousands of complaints</a> without investigation and raising urgent questions about who will enforce federal special education laws when states fall short. </p>

<p>And while large caseloads, according to disability rights advocates, are not new for the Office for Civil Rights, parents at least used to receive confirmation that their complaint was received and being looked at. Today, however, it is not uncommon for parents to not receive confirmation – or any follow-ups to their case – even after it’s been dismissed. </p>

<p>Piñón’s <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1amPaTzSttVj992KB8IbAMeu8KupW8II3I4EKVHCSvNc/edit?tab=t.0">complaint was rejected in July 2024</a>, denied access to this link before President Donald Trump took office and ushered in the cuts at the Department of Education. It wasn’t the outcome she wanted, but it did provide her with important information and closure, and gave her comfort that she had a place to turn.</p>

<p>“Even though the department wasn’t perfect,” Piñón told me, “they still provided an extra layer of rights, guidance and technical assistance for schools and districts.”  </p>

<p><a href="https://education.utexas.edu/faculty/david_dematthews/">As a teacher</a> and district administrator in West Baltimore and in Washington, I’ve seen firsthand how difficult it can be for states, districts and schools to implement special education law on their own. And now as a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ekLOu04AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">professor and researcher</a> at the University of Texas, I focus much of my work on improving schools for students with disabilities. I have talked to parents, advocates and school officials, many of whom are greatly concerned that cuts to the OCR will be harmful.</p>

<p>For parents like Piñón, the question now is not whether the system has ever worked perfectly, but whether families can continue to look to the Education Department and the Office for Civil Rights for support when states, districts and schools fail to meet their obligations in giving all children a quality education.</p>
